title: Moon phases and eclipses: how much of the Moon is lit, and where a shadow ends

summary.text: The Moon's dark shadow only just reaches the Earth, and in some months it falls short. So why are total solar eclipses rare? In this lesson you will measure how much of a sock Moon is lit at seven places, and find where the dark shadow of a seed ends.
summary.art: A table at night under one round bulb: a child lifts a peppercorn on a thin stick above white paper, and the small shadow below has a dark middle with a pale grey ring round it.

intro.hook: The Sun is about 400 times as wide as the Moon. So how can the small Moon cover the whole Sun in a solar eclipse? And why does it sometimes leave a bright ring of Sun showing?
intro.text: In this lesson you answer both questions with a coin, a plate and a lamp. First you hide a steel plate behind a coin. Then you measure how much of a model Moon is lit at seven places on its path. You lift seeds under a lamp and find where each dark shadow ends. At the end you can say why eclipses are rare and why the eclipsed Moon turns red. You can also say how people measured the Earth with a shadow.
intro.art: A child with one eye closed holding a coin at arm's length, so that the coin exactly covers a round steel plate propped on a shelf across the room.

outcomes: By the end I can explain the Moon's phases and the two pakshas, and say why phases are not the Earth's shadow.
By the end I can use the Moon's angle from the Sun to say how much of its face is lit.
By the end I can explain that moonlight is reflected sunlight, and why the dark Moon looks white.
By the end I can tell the umbra from the penumbra, and use the rule for where a dark shadow ends.
By the end I can explain total, partial and ring solar eclipses, using the Moon's shadow and its distance.
By the end I can explain a lunar eclipse, why the Moon turns red, and who can see it.
By the end I can explain why eclipses do not come every month, and find the pattern of eclipse seasons.
By the end I can tell how eclipses were used to measure the Earth and the Moon, and how to watch one safely.

terms.meaning: The shape of the lit part of the Moon that we see on one night. The Moon itself stays a whole round ball.
terms.example: A thin crescent, a half Moon and a full Moon are three phases.
terms.art: Eight small Moons in a row, from a thin crescent to a full circle and back to a thin crescent.

terms.meaning: The night when the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun. Its lit half faces away from us, so we see no Moon.
terms.example: Diwali falls on Amavasya, the darkest night of its month.
terms.art: The Sun on the left, the Earth on the right and the Moon between them, with the Moon's lit half facing the Sun.

terms.meaning: The night when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. We see the whole lit half of the Moon.
terms.example: On Purnima the Moon rises in the east as the Sun sets in the west.
terms.art: A full Moon rising over rooftops on one side of the sky while the sky on the other side is orange from sunset.

terms.meaning: The bright fortnight, from Amavasya to Purnima. The lit part of the Moon that we see grows each night.
terms.example: Three days into Shukla Paksha, a thin crescent shows in the west after sunset.
terms.art: A row of seven Moons growing from a thin crescent to a full circle, with an arrow pointing from thin to full.

terms.meaning: The dark fortnight, from Purnima to Amavasya. The lit part of the Moon that we see shrinks each night.
terms.example: A week into Krishna Paksha, a half Moon rises near midnight.
terms.art: A row of seven Moons shrinking from a full circle to a thin crescent, with an arrow pointing from full to thin.

terms.meaning: Light that falls on a thing and bounces off it. The Moon makes no light. Moonlight is sunlight that has bounced off the Moon.
terms.example: A white wall in sunshine lights up a shady room with reflected light.
terms.art: An arrow of light going from the Sun to the Moon, and a second, thinner arrow going from the Moon to a child's eye on the Earth.

terms.meaning: The share of the light falling on a surface that the surface sends back. It is given as parts in every 100.
terms.example: Fresh snow sends back about 85 parts in every 100. The Moon sends back about 12.
terms.art: Three squares side by side, white, grey and nearly black, each with a thick arrow of light coming in and a thinner arrow going out.

terms.meaning: How far apart the Moon and the Sun are in our sky, measured in degrees. It grows by about 12 degrees each day after Amavasya.
terms.example: At a half Moon the angle is 90 degrees. At Purnima it is 180 degrees.
terms.art: A child at the centre of a half circle, with one arm pointing to the setting Sun and the other to a half Moon, and the angle between the arms marked 90 degrees.

terms.meaning: What happens when one body in space moves into the shadow of another. The Sun, the Earth and the Moon must be in one straight line.
terms.example: On 7 September 2025 the Moon passed through the Earth's shadow, and people across India saw a lunar eclipse.
terms.art: The Sun, the Earth and the Moon drawn in one straight line, with a long dark shadow stretching behind the Earth.

terms.meaning: An eclipse in which the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth. The Moon's shadow falls on part of the Earth. It can only happen at Amavasya.
terms.example: On 22 July 2009 a total solar eclipse crossed India from Surat to Patna.
terms.art: The Moon between the Sun and the Earth, with a small dark spot of shadow on the Earth's surface.

terms.meaning: An eclipse in which the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon. The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. It can only happen at Purnima.
terms.example: In a total lunar eclipse the whole Moon is inside the Earth's shadow, and it turns a dark red.
terms.art: The Earth between the Sun and the Moon, with the Moon sitting inside the Earth's long dark shadow and coloured dull red.

terms.meaning: The dark middle of a shadow. From inside the umbra, the whole lamp or the whole Sun is hidden.
terms.example: People standing in the Moon's umbra see a total solar eclipse.
terms.art: The shadow of a small ball on white paper, with the dark middle marked by an arrow.

terms.meaning: The paler ring round the dark middle of a shadow. From inside the penumbra, part of the lamp or part of the Sun still shows.
terms.example: People standing in the Moon's penumbra see a partial solar eclipse.
terms.art: The shadow of a small ball on white paper, with the pale grey ring round the dark middle marked by an arrow.

terms.meaning: The part of an eclipse when the Sun or the Moon is completely covered. In a solar eclipse it never lasts longer than about seven and a half minutes.
terms.example: At Varanasi on 22 July 2009, totality lasted about three minutes.
terms.art: A black disc in a dark sky with a pale, feathery white glow spreading out all round it.

terms.meaning: A solar eclipse in which the Moon is too far from the Earth to cover the whole Sun. A bright ring of Sun shows round the Moon. Annular means ring-shaped.
terms.example: On 26 December 2019 people in Coimbatore, Ooty and Kannur saw a ring of Sun.
terms.art: A black disc in the sky with a thin, even, bright ring of Sun all the way round it.

terms.meaning: The Sun's faint outer layer of very hot, thin gas. It is always there, but the Sun's glare hides it. It shows only when the Sun's bright face is covered.
terms.example: In totality the corona appears as a pale white glow round the black Moon.
terms.art: The black disc of the Moon with long pale streamers of white light reaching out on both sides.

terms.meaning: One of the two points where the Moon's tilted path crosses the Earth's path round the Sun. Eclipses happen only near a node. Indian astronomers named the two nodes Rahu and Ketu.
terms.example: If Purnima comes when the Moon is near a node, there is a lunar eclipse.
terms.art: Two rings tilted a little against each other, crossing at two points marked with small crosses.

terms.meaning: A stretch of about five weeks when the Sun is near a node, so eclipses can happen. Eclipse seasons come about every six Moon months.
terms.example: In 2026 the eclipse seasons were in February and March, and again in August.
terms.art: A strip calendar of one year with two short coloured bands, one near March and one near September, each holding two small eclipse signs.

explanations.definition: The Moon makes no light of its own. The Sun lights it, and some of that sunlight bounces off the Moon to our eyes.
explanations.description: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach the Moon. The Moon's ground sends back about 12 parts in every 100 of that light. The reflected light reaches the Earth about 1.3 seconds later. Very little of the Sun's light takes this path. So the full Moon is about 400,000 times dimmer than the Sun. That is why you can look at the Moon for as long as you like, and must never look at the Sun. The Earth reflects sunlight too. Seen from the Moon, the full Earth shines more than 40 times as brightly as the full Moon shines for us.
examples: The Sun, a lamp and a firefly make their own light.
The Moon, the planets and a white wall only reflect light.
Moonlight is sunlight that left the Sun about eight and a half minutes earlier.
explanations.art: The Sun on the left sending a wide beam to the Moon, and a much thinner beam going from the Moon down to a child at a window on the Earth.

explanations.definition: The Sun always lights the half of the Moon that faces it. The Moon goes round the Earth, so we see a different share of that lit half each night.
explanations.description: At Amavasya the Moon is between us and the Sun. Its lit half faces away from us, and we see nothing. Over the next two weeks the Moon moves round the Earth, and we see more of the lit half each night. This fortnight is Shukla Paksha. At Purnima the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, and we see the whole lit half. Then the lit part shrinks through Krishna Paksha. One full round, from Amavasya to Amavasya, takes about 29 and a half days. The phases are not made by the Earth's shadow. The Earth's shadow touches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse. A crescent Moon is often in the sky beside the Sun, where the Earth's shadow cannot reach.
examples: At Amavasya, the lit half of the Moon faces away from the Earth.
At a half Moon, we see half of the lit half. That is a quarter of the whole ball.
At Purnima, the whole lit half of the Moon faces the Earth.
explanations.art: The Earth in the middle with eight Moons round it, every Moon lit on the side facing the Sun, and beside each one a small picture of the shape seen from the Earth.

explanations.concept: How much of the Moon is lit: the angle rule
explanations.definition: The share of the Moon's face that looks lit depends on the angle between the Moon and the Sun in our sky. It is 0 at 0 degrees, half at 90 degrees and all at 180 degrees.
explanations.description: In How Much of the Moon Is Lit, a ball half covered by a dark sock stood at seven places round a viewer. At 30 degrees from the Sun, only about 7 parts in 100 of its face looked lit. At 60 degrees it was 25, at 90 degrees 50, at 120 degrees 75, and at 150 degrees about 93. The lit share does not grow evenly. It grows slowly near Amavasya and near Purnima, and fastest near the half Moon. The reason is the direction we look from. Near Amavasya the lit half is turned almost fully away, and we see only its edge. The Moon moves about 12 degrees further from the Sun each day. So the angle tells you the phase, and the phase tells you the angle.
examples: About 2 and a half days after Amavasya, the Moon is 30 degrees from the Sun. About 7 parts in 100 of its face are lit.
About 7 and a half days after Amavasya, the Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun. It looks like a half Moon.
The shares at 60 and 120 degrees add up to 100. So do the shares at 30 and 150 degrees.
explanations.art: A half circle with a viewer at its centre and seven balls spaced along it, each ball half bare and half covered in dark cloth, with the percent lit written beside each ball: 0, 7, 25, 50, 75, 93, 100.

explanations.concept: The Moon is dark, but it looks white
explanations.definition: The Moon's ground is dark grey. It reflects about 12 parts in every 100 of the light that falls on it, about the same as an old tar road.
explanations.description: In A Black Card in the Dark, a black card lit alone in a dark room looked pale grey or even white. When a white strip came into the same light, the card looked black again. Our eyes judge how light a thing is by comparing it with what is near it. The Moon hangs in a black sky, with nothing brighter beside it. So the brightest thing we can see looks white. In the daytime sky the same Moon looks pale and dull beside a sunlit cloud. Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the Moon, said its dust stuck to his boots like powdered charcoal.
examples: Fresh snow reflects about 85 parts in 100, and white paper about 80.
The Earth, with its clouds and seas, reflects about 30 parts in 100.
The Moon reflects about 12 parts in 100, and charcoal about 4.
explanations.art: A full Moon in a black sky looking bright white on the left, and on the right the same Moon as a dull grey disc beside a bright white cloud in a blue sky.

explanations.concept: A shadow has a dark middle, a pale ring and an end
explanations.definition: A shadow made by a wide light has two parts. The umbra is the dark middle, where the whole light is hidden. The penumbra is the pale ring, where part of the light still shows. The umbra gets narrower with distance and ends at a point.
explanations.description: In The Shadow That Runs Out, you lifted a seed above paper under a lamp. The dark middle of its shadow shrank and then vanished, and only a pale smudge was left. A seed twice as wide had a dark shadow twice as long. The rule was the same for every seed. Divide the lamp's distance by the lamp's width, and you get the length of the dark shadow in seed-widths. The Sun is about 108 Sun-widths away from us. So in sunlight every dark shadow ends about 108 widths behind the thing that makes it. The shadow is a cone of darkness in space, with its tip pointing away from the Sun.
examples: A peppercorn 5 millimetres wide has a dark shadow about 54 centimetres long in sunlight.
The Moon is 3,474 kilometres wide. Its dark shadow is about 375,000 kilometres long.
The Earth is 12,742 kilometres wide. Its dark shadow is about 1.4 million kilometres long.
explanations.art: A wide round lamp on the left and a small ball in the middle, with a dark cone narrowing to a point behind the ball and a paler, widening cone round it.

explanations.concept: A solar eclipse is the tip of the Moon's shadow
explanations.definition: In a total solar eclipse, the tip of the Moon's umbra touches the Earth. Only people inside that small dark spot see the Sun fully covered.
explanations.description: The Moon's dark shadow is about 375,000 kilometres long. The ground below the Moon is about that far away. So only the narrow tip of the cone reaches the Earth. The dark spot on the ground is never more than about 270 kilometres wide. It moves across the Earth at more than 1,000 kilometres an hour, along a strip called the path of totality. At any one place, totality lasts a few minutes, and never longer than about seven and a half. Round the dark spot lies the penumbra, thousands of kilometres wide. People there see a partial eclipse, with a bite taken out of the Sun. Everyone else sees no eclipse.
examples: Someone standing inside the umbra sees a total eclipse. The sky is dark and the corona shows.
Someone standing inside the penumbra sees a partial eclipse. Part of the Sun is still bright.
Any one town sees a total solar eclipse about once in 375 years, on average.
explanations.art: The Moon between the Sun and the Earth, with a thin dark cone from the Moon ending in a tiny spot on the Earth, and a wide pale cone round it covering a large patch of the Earth.

explanations.concept: Total or ring: the Moon's distance changes
explanations.definition: The Moon's path round the Earth is a slightly stretched circle. When the Moon is near, its dark shadow reaches the ground and the eclipse is total. When it is far, the shadow ends above the ground and a ring of Sun is left.
explanations.description: In The Coin Eclipse, a coin near your eye hid the whole plate. When you moved the coin a little further away, a ring of plate showed round it. The Moon does the same. Its centre is on average about 363,000 kilometres from the Earth's centre at its nearest, and about 405,000 at its furthest. The Sun is about 400 times as wide as the Moon, and about 390 times as far away. So the two look almost exactly the same size in our sky. A near Moon looks a little bigger than the Sun, and covers it. A far Moon looks a little smaller. Then people on the centre line see an annular eclipse, a ring of Sun round a black Moon. The sky stays bright and the corona stays hidden.
examples: A total solar eclipse was seen on 22 July 2009 from Surat, Varanasi and Patna.
A ring eclipse was seen on 26 December 2019 from Kannur, Ooty and Coimbatore.
Another ring eclipse was seen on 15 January 2010 from Kanyakumari and Rameswaram.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a black Moon exactly covering the Sun with a pale glow round it, and a slightly smaller black Moon with a thin bright ring of Sun round it.

explanations.concept: A lunar eclipse: the Moon inside the Earth's shadow
explanations.definition: In a lunar eclipse the Moon passes through the Earth's shadow. It can happen only at Purnima, when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.
explanations.description: The Earth's dark shadow is about 1.4 million kilometres long, far longer than the distance to the Moon. Where the Moon crosses it, the dark shadow is still about 9,200 kilometres wide. That is about 2.6 times the width of the Moon. So the whole Moon can go inside, and it can stay there for up to about an hour and three-quarters. Everyone on the night side of the Earth can watch, because the shadow is on the Moon itself. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with bare eyes. If only part of the Moon enters the dark shadow, the eclipse is partial. If the Moon passes only through the pale penumbra, it dims so little that most people notice nothing.
examples: In a total lunar eclipse, the whole Moon is inside the umbra.
In a partial lunar eclipse, a curved dark edge covers part of the Moon.
In a penumbral lunar eclipse, the Moon is only in the pale outer shadow.
explanations.art: The Earth with a long dark cone behind it, and the Moon drawn three times crossing the cone: entering, fully inside and coloured dull red, and leaving.

explanations.concept: Why the eclipsed Moon turns red
explanations.definition: During a total lunar eclipse a little sunlight still reaches the Moon. The Earth's air bends this light into the shadow, and the air lets mostly red light through.
explanations.description: The Earth's air works like a thin lens all round the planet. Sunlight that skims through the air is bent inwards, into the Earth's shadow. On the way, the air scatters most of the blue light out sideways. The same thing reddens the Sun at sunrise and sunset. So the light that reaches the Moon is the red light of every sunrise and sunset on the Earth at that moment. An astronaut on the Moon would see the black Earth cover the Sun, with a thin red ring of glowing air round it. The colour changes from one eclipse to the next. When a big volcano has filled the high air with dust, less light gets through. After Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, the eclipsed Moon of December 1992 was so dark that it almost vanished.
examples: When the high air is clear, the eclipsed Moon is a bright copper-red or orange.
When the high air is dusty after a volcano, the eclipsed Moon is dark brown or grey.
Astronomers rate the brightness from 0 to 4 on the Danjon scale, made by Andre Danjon in 1921.
explanations.art: The Earth seen from the Moon as a black disc with a thin glowing red-orange ring all round its edge, and the Moon's grey ground in the front lit dull red.

explanations.concept: Why there is not an eclipse every month
explanations.definition: The Moon's path is tilted about 5 degrees against the Earth's path round the Sun. So at most Amavasyas and Purnimas, the Moon passes above or below the straight line, and the shadows miss.
explanations.description: The two paths cross at two points, called nodes. Indian astronomers named them Rahu and Ketu. An eclipse happens only when Amavasya or Purnima comes while the Moon is near a node. The Sun lines up with a node about every 173 days. Around that time there is an eclipse season of about five weeks. Every season has at least one solar eclipse and one lunar eclipse, about two weeks apart. In Eclipse Detective, the 12 eclipses of 2024, 2025 and 2026 fell into six seasons. Each season came about six Moon months after the one before. The seasons come about 19 days earlier each year, because the nodes slowly slide round the Moon's path.
examples: A year has 12 or 13 Purnimas, but only 2 or 3 lunar eclipses.
The eclipses of 2025 came in March and in September.
The eclipses of 2026 came in February and March, and in August.
explanations.art: Two rings tilted slightly against each other and crossing at two marked points, with the Moon drawn above the line at one full Moon and exactly on the line at another.

explanations.definition: After 18 years and about 11 days, the Sun, the Moon and the node come back to almost the same places. So each eclipse is followed by a very similar one after that time. This cycle is called the saros.
explanations.description: Sky-watchers in Babylon, in today's Iraq, found this pattern more than 2,000 years ago from long lists of eclipses written on clay tablets. They could say when to expect an eclipse without knowing what caused it. The total solar eclipse of 29 March 2006 was followed by a similar one on 8 April 2024. The next in that family comes on 20 April 2042. The extra third of a day in the cycle lets the Earth turn a third of the way round. So each eclipse in the family falls about a third of the way round the world from the last. Today astronomers work out the Moon's path so exactly that eclipses are known to the second, hundreds of years ahead.
examples: One saros is 223 Moon months, which is 18 years and about 11 days.
29 March 2006, 8 April 2024 and 20 April 2042 are three total solar eclipses in one family.
India's Aryabhata gave rules in 499 CE for working out the time and size of an eclipse.
explanations.art: A row of three small Earth globes, each with a curved dark eclipse path drawn across a different part of the globe, labelled 2006, 2024 and 2042.

explanations.concept: Measuring the Earth, the Moon and the Sun with eclipses
explanations.definition: The Earth's shadow on the Moon is always curved like part of a circle. Its size, compared with the Moon, shows how big the Earth is compared with the Moon.
explanations.description: About 2,400 years ago the Greek thinker Aristotle pointed out that the Earth's shadow on the Moon is round in every lunar eclipse. Only a ball throws a round shadow from every side. So the Earth is a ball. Some decades later Aristarchus of Samos compared the curve of the shadow with the Moon. In Fit the Earth's Shadow you did the same with a photograph. The shadow is about 2.6 Moons wide. It has narrowed by about one Moon-width on its way to the Moon. So the Earth is about 3.6 Moons wide. The real figure is 3.7. Aristarchus also tried to measure the Sun's distance from the angle of the half Moon. In Aristarchus's Angle you saw why that failed. The angle is too close to 90 degrees to measure by eye.
examples: The Earth is 12,742 kilometres wide and the Moon is 3,474. The Earth is 3.7 times as wide.
The shadow's curved edge fits a circle about 2.6 Moons wide.
Aristarchus's angle was 87 degrees. The true angle is 89.85 degrees.
explanations.art: A partly eclipsed Moon with the curved edge of the Earth's shadow on it, and a large faint circle drawn to continue that curve, about 2.6 times as wide as the Moon.

explanations.concept: What a total solar eclipse shows: the corona
explanations.definition: The corona is the Sun's outer layer of thin gas. It is hotter than a million degrees Celsius, far hotter than the Sun's bright surface below it, which is about 5,500 degrees.
explanations.description: The corona is about a million times fainter than the Sun's face. So it shows only when the Moon covers that face exactly. In the last seconds before totality, sunlight shines through valleys on the Moon's edge as a row of bright dots. They are called Baily's beads. Then the sky darkens, bright stars and planets appear, and the corona spreads out round the black Moon. Until the 1930s, total eclipses were the only way to study the corona. Now spacecraft block the Sun with a disc of their own. India's Aditya-L1 carries such an instrument. Nobody yet knows for certain why the corona is so hot.
examples: On 29 July 1878 the American astronomer Maria Mitchell took five of her students from Vassar College to Denver to watch the eclipse.
On 22 January 1898 Annie Maunder photographed the corona from Talni in Maharashtra. Her picture showed one of the longest streamers of light seen up to that time.
Helium was first found in light from the Sun's edge, in the eclipse of 18 August 1868, seen from Guntur.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study waves in the Sun's gas
perspectives.explanation: The Sun's magnetic field shakes like a plucked string. These waves carry energy up from the surface and give it to the corona as heat.
Millions of tiny explosions, called nanoflares, go off all the time where magnetic lines snap and join again. Together they keep the corona hot. Eugene Parker suggested this in 1988.

explanations.art: The black disc of the Moon with a row of tiny bright beads along one edge, and pale white streamers of the corona stretching out on both sides.

explanations.definition: Never look at the Sun, eclipse or no eclipse. Looking at a lunar eclipse is completely safe.
explanations.description: Even when most of the Sun is covered, the part that still shows can burn the back of the eye. It does not hurt while it happens, because that part of the eye has no pain nerves. Sunglasses, smoked glass, X-ray film and water in a bowl are not safe. Use eclipse glasses marked ISO 12312-2, and check them for scratches first. You can also watch without looking up at all. Small gaps between the leaves of a tree throw tiny pictures of the Sun on the ground. During a partial eclipse each round patch turns into a crescent. During an annular eclipse each patch turns into a ring. Eating, drinking and going outdoors during an eclipse are safe. An eclipse is a shadow, and a shadow adds nothing to the air, the water or the food.
examples: These are safe: eclipse glasses marked ISO 12312-2, and the patches of light under a tree.
These are not safe: sunglasses, X-ray film, smoked glass, or a camera or binoculars without a proper filter.
A lunar eclipse needs no protection at all.
explanations.art: The ground under a leafy tree covered with hundreds of small crescent-shaped patches of light, and a child pointing down at them with their back to the Sun.

agreed.text: The Moon shines only by reflected sunlight, and the Sun always lights half of it.
agreed.evidence: The lit side of the Moon always points towards the Sun. Spacecraft that go round the Moon photograph its day side and its night side, as we do for the Earth.

agreed.text: The Moon's phases come from the direction we see it from, and not from the Earth's shadow.
agreed.evidence: A crescent Moon is seen close to the Sun in the sky, where the Earth's shadow cannot fall. A half-covered ball shows every phase when you only change where you stand.

agreed.text: A solar eclipse is the Moon's shadow on the Earth, and a lunar eclipse is the Earth's shadow on the Moon.
agreed.evidence: Eclipses are worked out from the paths of the Earth and the Moon, and they arrive on time to the second. Satellites have photographed the Moon's dark spot crossing the Earth.

agreed.text: The Moon's dark shadow is about 375,000 kilometres long, so its tip only just reaches the Earth.
agreed.evidence: The dark spot on the ground is never more than about 270 kilometres wide. When the Moon is far away, the eclipse is a ring and no dark spot reaches the ground.

agreed.text: The eclipsed Moon is red because sunlight is bent and reddened by the Earth's air.
agreed.evidence: The eclipsed Moon is darker after big volcanic eruptions, when the high air is dusty. Japan's Kaguya spacecraft, going round the Moon, filmed the Earth covering the Sun in February 2009, with a bright ring of air round it.

challenging.claim: A half Moon gives half as much light as a full Moon.
challenging.for: At a half Moon, half of the Moon's face is lit. So it seems that half the light should reach us.
challenging.against: Measurements show that a half Moon gives only about one-tenth of the light of a full Moon. At a half Moon, sunlight hits the rough ground from the side, and long shadows cover much of it. At a full Moon the shadows are hidden behind the things that cast them.
challenging.context: This card is about how bright the Moon is at different phases.

challenging.claim: Solar eclipses are much rarer than lunar eclipses.
challenging.for: Most people have seen several lunar eclipses and no total solar eclipse. So solar eclipses seem rare.
challenging.against: Counted over the whole Earth, there are about 240 solar eclipses in a century. There are only about 150 lunar eclipses in which the dark shadow touches the Moon. A lunar eclipse is seen from half the Earth. A total solar eclipse is seen only from a strip up to about 270 kilometres wide.
challenging.context: This card is about which kind of eclipse happens more often.

challenging.claim: The Sun is far bigger than the Earth, so the Earth must go round the Sun.
challenging.who: Aristarchus of Samos, about 2,300 years ago
challenging.for: Aristarchus used eclipses and the half Moon to show that the Sun is much bigger than the Earth. He reasoned that the smaller body should circle the larger one.
challenging.against: Almost nobody agreed with him at the time. People could not feel the Earth move. They also saw no shift in the stars through the year, which a moving Earth should cause. That shift is real, but far too small to see without a telescope.
challenging.context: This card is about an idea that came out of measuring eclipses, and was ignored for about 1,800 years.

challenging.claim: Thales of Miletus predicted the solar eclipse of 28 May 585 BCE.
challenging.who: The Greek historian Herodotus, writing about 150 years later
challenging.for: Herodotus wrote that Thales had told people the year of the eclipse in advance. The eclipse itself is real, and astronomers can work out its date.
challenging.against: Nobody in 585 BCE knew a method that could say where a solar eclipse would be seen. Many historians think the story grew in the telling, or that Thales made a lucky guess.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous story of the first eclipse prediction.

challenging.claim: Animals know that a solar eclipse is coming before it starts.
challenging.for: People report birds going to roost and cattle walking home as the light fades. In the total eclipse of 21 August 2017, microphones in flower fields showed that bees stopped flying during totality.
challenging.against: The bees kept flying through the partial part and stopped only when the sky went dark. So far the careful studies show animals answering the change in light. They have not shown any animal sensing an eclipse in advance.
challenging.context: This card is about what other animals do during a solar eclipse, and what has really been measured.

big_questions.q: A shadow is a place where light is missing. Is a shadow a thing, or the lack of a thing?
big_questions.hint: Think of The Shadow That Runs Out. The dark shadow had a width, a length and a tip that you could measure.

big_questions.q: The Moon is as dark as an old tar road, but everyone calls it white. Who is right?

story.title: The Morning That Did Not Go Dark
story.note: A made-up story. Yazhini, Kathir, Aaya and Shanthi Miss are imagined, and so is everything they say and do. The annular eclipse of 26 December 2019 is real. In Coimbatore the ring lasted about three minutes, a little before half past nine in the morning. That week the Earth was close to its nearest point to the Sun, and the Moon was not at its nearest to the Earth. So the Moon looked a little smaller than the Sun. Gaps between leaves really do throw ring-shaped pictures of the Sun on the ground during such an eclipse. Aaya is a word for grandmother used in parts of Tamil Nadu. Many families used to stay indoors during an eclipse. An eclipse harms nobody who does not look at the Sun.
text: On Christmas night in 2019, all of Coimbatore seemed to be talking about the Sun. The next morning, a little before half past nine, the Moon would pass in front of it.
Yazhini was ten. Her cousin Kathir, who was seven, had come for the holidays, and he knew exactly what was going to happen.
"It goes dark," he said. "Completely dark. The stars come out in the morning and the birds go to sleep. I saw it in a book."
"Not tomorrow," said Yazhini. "Shanthi Miss told us. Tomorrow is a ring eclipse. A ring of Sun stays all round the Moon. It won't go dark."
"Why not?" said Kathir. "The Moon covered the whole Sun in my book. Has the Moon become smaller since then?"

Yazhini opened her mouth and shut it again. She did not know. The Moon could not shrink. But her teacher had said a ring. She had given every child a card viewer with a square of dark film in it, and had told them never to look at the Sun without it.

Aaya, their grandmother, was shelling groundnuts on the floor. "There was an eclipse when I was a girl," she said. "My mother shut every window, and we sat inside until it was over. I have never seen one in my life." She did not sound pleased about it.

After dinner Yazhini sat on the swing in the long front room and thought about Kathir's question. On the far wall hung the round clock, as wide as a steel plate. On the shelf beside her lay a five-rupee coin.
She shut one eye and held the coin out at the full length of her arm. The coin sat in the middle of the clock like a dark button. The white face of the clock showed all round it, in a ring.
"Let me," said Kathir. He climbed onto the swing beside her, shut one eye and held the coin out. "It covers the whole clock," he said. "There's no ring. You're doing it wrong."
"I am not." She took the coin back and saw a ring. She gave it to him, and he saw no ring. It was the same coin and the same clock, and they were sitting on the same swing.
She looked at his arm, stretched out next to hers. His fist reached only as far as her wrist.
"Don't move," she said. She took hold of his hand and drew it slowly forward, until the coin was level with her own fingers. "Now look."
"Oh," said Kathir. "There's a ring."

So that was it. The coin had not changed. It was only further from his eye, and a thing that is further away looks smaller. When the coin was further away, it left a ring. When it was nearer, it covered the clock.
Yazhini sat very still. Then the Moon did not have to shrink. It only had to be further away. But was the Moon ever further away than usual?

She ran to her school bag and pulled out the sheet that Shanthi Miss had given them. She had not read past the first line. Near the bottom it said that the Moon's path round the Earth is not a perfect circle. In some weeks the Moon is nearer to us, and in some weeks it is further. This week it was on the far part of its path.
"Kathir," she said, "your book and my teacher are both right." She explained it to him with the coin, twice, until he could explain it back to her.

In the morning the terrace was full of neighbours, passing viewers from hand to hand. Through the dark film the Sun was a small pale disc with a black bite out of one side. The bite grew. Aaya stayed downstairs in the doorway with her groundnuts.

By nine o'clock the light had gone strange. It was not dark. It was thin, like the light before a storm, and the shadows of the railings were very sharp. The air felt cooler on Yazhini's arms. The crows on the water tank had gone quiet.
Then, a little before half past nine, the black Moon slid right inside the Sun and did not cover it. All round the Moon there was a thin, even, burning ring.
"It's too far away," whispered Kathir, with the viewer pressed to his face. "It can't reach the edges."
Yazhini handed her viewer to the girl next door and ran down the stairs. "Aaya, come out. You don't have to look up. Look down."

Under the neem tree by the gate, the ground was covered with rings. There were hundreds of them, small and bright. They lay on the swept earth and on the white veshti drying on the line, wherever sunlight came through a gap in the leaves. Each one was a little picture of the Sun, with the Moon in the middle of it.
Aaya came out slowly, with the end of her sari over her head. She looked at the ground for a long time. Then she put out her hand, and a ring lay in her palm.
"Sixty years I sat inside," she said. "And it was a thing like this."

The rings lasted nearly three minutes. Then each one broke on one side and became a thin crescent, and the crescents began, very slowly, to grow fat again. Upstairs somebody cheered. Kathir came running down to tell Aaya that it had not gone dark, as if he had known all along.
Yazhini kept the coin. That night she held it up against the clock once more, at the end of her arm, and looked at the white ring round it.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes on the swing. The same coin covers the clock for Kathir and leaves a ring for Yazhini, because his arm is shorter and the coin is nearer his eye. Yazhini sees that the Moon need not shrink to leave a ring. It only has to be further away. The story shows why some solar eclipses are total and some are rings. It also shows the eclipse watched safely, with a viewer and with the patches of light under a tree.
ask: Why did the same coin leave a ring for Yazhini and cover the whole clock for Kathir?
What has to be true of the Moon for a solar eclipse to leave a ring of Sun?
Why did the morning not go dark, though most of the Sun was covered?
Why were the patches of light under the neem tree shaped like rings?
Aaya had stayed indoors for every eclipse of her life. What would you tell someone who is afraid of an eclipse?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people first measure the Moon and the Sun without leaving the ground? This card tells the true story, and one answer that stayed wrong for nearly 2,000 years.
how_we_found_out.story: About 2,300 years ago, on the Greek island of Samos, Aristarchus tried to measure the sky with eclipses. During a lunar eclipse he watched the Earth's curved shadow cross the Moon. He judged that the shadow was about two Moons wide. From that he worked out that the Moon is roughly a third as wide as the Earth, which was close. Then he measured the angle between the half Moon and the Sun as 87 degrees. From this he worked out that the Sun is about 19 times as far away as the Moon. That number for the Sun's distance was wrong, but astronomers repeated it for nearly 2,000 years. His method was sound. The true angle is 89.85 degrees, and no eye can tell that from 90. In 1672 Giovanni Cassini in Paris and Jean Richer in South America measured the position of Mars from two places at the same time. Their result put the Sun about 140 million kilometres away. So the Sun is about 390 times as far away as the Moon.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristarchus of Samos, and later Giovanni Cassini and Jean Richer
how_we_found_out.when: Aristarchus worked about 270 BCE. Cassini and Richer measured Mars in 1672.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the Sun is only about 19 times as far away as the Moon. Measurements of Mars from two places in 1672 showed that the Sun is about 390 times as far.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in ancient Greek dress on a hillside at dawn, holding two sticks joined at one end, one pointing at a half Moon high in the sky and the other at the place where the Sun is rising.

roots.context: We have learned how the Moon's phases and eclipses work, and that a dark shadow has a length and a tip. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In The Shadow That Runs Out, the dark middle of every shadow shrank to a point and ended. A shadow is a cone of space behind a thing, and it has a tip. The Moon's dark cone is about 375,000 kilometres long, and the Earth is about that far away. So a total solar eclipse is the tip of a shadow just touching the ground.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a shadow as a flat dark patch on a floor or a wall. The patch is only the slice where a surface cuts through the shadow. The shadow fills the space behind the thing, even where nothing is there to show it.
deep_truth.evidence: Take a bulb 6 centimetres wide, 180 centimetres above the paper. A peppercorn's dark shadow ends about 15 centimetres below the peppercorn, and a chana's about 24 centimetres below. Above and below the paper the shadow was still there, in the air. In sunlight the rule gives 108 widths. For the Moon that is 3,474 times 108, which is about 375,000 kilometres.

three.who_am_i: Every evening the turning Earth carries you into the Earth's own shadow, and every morning it carries you out. Night is simply the time when your side of the Earth is inside that shadow. The shadow is a dark cone in space, about 1.4 million kilometres long.
three.what_is_life: When the Moon's shadow passes, bees stop flying and birds go to roost. Living beings read the light all day long, and answer when it changes.
three.what_is_this_world: Every planet and every moon has a dark cone of shadow behind it, pointing away from the Sun. We notice a cone only when something moves into it.

roots.thread: The Sun, the Moon and the Earth are three separate bodies. An eclipse happens only when all three stand in one line, and then one shadow joins them. The red light on the eclipsed Moon has passed through the Earth's air, at every place where the Sun is rising or setting. So the Moon, the Earth's air and the Sun all take part in one event. When we see the Moon turn red, we are seeing the light of sunrises and sunsets that are happening on the Earth at that very moment.

teachings.source: Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya (499 CE), Golapada, the verses on eclipses
teachings.teaching: The Moon covers the Sun, and the great shadow of the Earth covers the Moon.
teachings.link: Aryabhata treated the Earth's shadow as a real thing with a size, reaching out into space. From its size he worked out how long an eclipse would last.

teachings.teaching: Penumbra asks Shadow why it keeps moving and stopping, and has no will of its own. Shadow answers that it depends on something else, and that thing may depend on something else again.
teachings.link: In The Shadow That Runs Out, the dark shadow depended on the seed, the lamp and the distance between them. Change any one, and the shadow changed.

science.text: Eclipses are worked out from the sizes, distances and paths of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon. The predictions are right to within a second, hundreds of years ahead.
The Sun's corona, which a total eclipse shows, is hotter than a million degrees. Why it is so much hotter than the surface below is still being worked out.

other_view.view: A shadow is not a thing at all. Only the light, the Moon and the Earth are real. The 'cone' is a way of saying which places the light does not reach. It has no weight, and it cannot push or pull anything.

practice.title: Lift the shadow
practice.say: Sit under one lamp with a sheet of white paper in front of you. Hold your hand flat, just above the paper. Look at its shadow, dark and sharp. Now lift your hand slowly while you breathe in. Watch the edges soften and the dark part shrink. Lower your hand slowly while you breathe out. Do this three times. Then hold your hand still, halfway up. Feel that the shadow fills the air between your hand and the paper.
practice.kid: Sit under a lamp with white paper. Hold your hand just above the paper. Lift it slowly as you breathe in. Watch the shadow go soft. Lower it as you breathe out. Do it three times.

ask: In The Shadow That Runs Out, the shadow was in the air above the paper before the paper showed it. Where is your own shadow when it falls on nothing?
The eclipsed Moon is lit by sunrises and sunsets that nobody on the Moon is watching. Does a sunset need someone to see it?
The Moon's shadow only just reaches the Earth. What would people know about the Sun if it had always stopped short?

experiments.title: How Much of the Moon Is Lit? Measure a sock Moon at seven places
experiments.context: In this experiment a ball half covered by a dark sock is your Moon. The bare half is the half the Sun lights. You put the ball at seven places round you, and measure how much of its face looks lit from the middle. You will find out whether a Moon one-third of the way to full looks one-third lit.
experiments.question: The Moon moves from the Sun's side of the sky to the opposite side in about 15 days. How much of its face looks lit at each step of the way? Does the lit share grow by the same amount at every step?
experiments.predict: Guess first. The seven places are 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150 and 180 degrees from the Sun. At 60 degrees the Moon has gone one-third of the way from new to full. Will one-third of its face look lit? Write a guess in percent for all seven places, and say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same ball and the same sock at every place. Keep the ball 1 metre from your eye every time. At every place, turn the ball so that the bare half faces the Sun wall flat on. Only the place of the ball changes. Measure each photo twice, because the edge of the sock can be hard to judge.

materials.item: a pale ball 6 to 8 cm wide, such as a sweet lime, an orange or a tennis ball
a dark sock, or a dark cloth, that stretches over half the ball
rubber bands
a string 1 metre long, and chalk or 8 small paper slips with sticky tape
a ruler marked in centimetres and millimetres
a steel tumbler to stand the ball on
a phone with a camera. If you have none, use the ruler held at arm's length
a sheet of paper with SUN written on it, and a clear floor about 2.5 metres by 1 metre, with a wall at one end

schedule.what: Make the sock Moon. Mark seven places on the floor. Guess. Photograph the ball at each place. Measure the photos, work out the percent lit and draw a graph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the seven places. Draw a line graph of percent lit against degrees from the Sun. Last, write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: percent of the ball's face that looked lit
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A sweet lime with a rubber band round its middle and a dark sock pulled over one half, exactly up to the rubber band.
setup.caption: 1. Put a rubber band round the middle of the ball. Pull the sock over one half, up to the band.

setup.art: A floor seen from above: a cross marked E, a wall with a paper sign saying SUN, and seven marks on a half circle 1 metre from E, labelled 0 to 180.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the Earth spot E. Mark seven places on a half circle 1 metre from E.

setup.art: The half-covered ball on an upturned steel tumbler at one floor mark, its bare half facing the wall with the SUN sign, and a phone on the floor at E pointing at the ball.
setup.caption: 3. Stand the ball on a tumbler at a mark. Turn the bare half to face the Sun wall. Take a photo from E.

setup.art: A phone screen showing a photo of the ball, part bare and part dark, with a ruler held across the middle of the ball on the screen.
setup.caption: 4. On the photo, measure the whole width of the ball and the width of the bare part.

flow.do: 1. Put a rubber band round the widest part of the ball, like a belt. 2. Pull the dark sock over one half of the ball, exactly up to the band. 3. Hold the sock in place with the second rubber band, twisted behind the ball. 4. Stick the paper marked SUN on a wall.
flow.say: This ball is our Moon. The bare half is the half the Sun lights. The sock is the Moon's night side. The Sun always lights the half that faces it.
flow.kid: Put a rubber band round the middle of the ball. Pull the sock over one half. The bare half is the sunlit half. The sock is the night half.
flow.parent: The edge of the sock must run round the widest part of the ball, so that exactly half is bare. If you have no sock, colour half of an old ball with a black marker.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Much of the Moon Is Lit. Here you make a model Moon from a ball and a dark sock.

flow.do: 1. Mark a spot E on the floor, about 1.5 metres from the Sun wall. This is the Earth. 2. Hold one end of the string on E. Mark the spot 1 metre from E, straight towards the wall. Write 0 on it. 3. Keep the string tight and swing it round. Make a mark every 52 cm along the curve. 4. Number the marks 30, 60, 90, 120, 150 and 180.
flow.say: You sit at E, on the Earth. The marks show where the Moon is on seven different days. Mark 0 is towards the Sun. Mark 180 is on the side away from the Sun.
flow.kid: Mark the Earth spot E. Use the string to mark a half circle. Make a mark every 52 cm. Number the marks from 0 to 180.
flow.parent: Marks 52 cm apart on a circle 1 metre from E are 30 degrees apart. Check the work. Mark 90 should be exactly sideways from E, and mark 180 should be opposite mark 0. If the room is small, use a string of 50 cm and marks 26 cm apart.
flow.context: This step of How Much of the Moon Is Lit marks the floor. You mark the Earth spot and seven places for the model Moon, each 30 degrees further from the Sun.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the seven marks. 2. Say that the Moon takes about 15 days to go from mark 0 to mark 180. 3. Ask for a guess, in percent, of how much of the face will look lit at each mark. 4. Write the seven guesses in the table, with the reason.
flow.say: At mark 60 the Moon has gone one-third of the way. Will one-third of its face look lit? What about mark 30, and mark 90? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how much of the ball will look lit at each mark. Give each guess in percent. Say why. Write your seven guesses.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: It will grow evenly, about 17 percent more at each mark. (A fair guess. The test will check it.)
At mark 90 it will be half, because we see the ball from the side.
It will be 0 at mark 0, because the bare half faces away from me.

flow.context: This step of How Much of the Moon Is Lit is for guessing. You guess the percent of the model Moon's face that will look lit at each of seven places.

flow.do: 1. Stand the tumbler upside down on mark 0 and put the ball on it. 2. Turn the ball so that the bare half faces the Sun wall, flat on. 3. Prop the phone on its side against a book on the floor at E. Point the camera at the ball and take a photo. 4. Do the same at marks 30, 60 and 90. Each time, turn the bare half to face the wall again.
flow.say: The Sun is so far away that its light comes from the same direction at every mark. So the bare half must face the wall each time. What do you see from the Earth?
flow.kid: Put the ball on mark 0. Turn the bare half to face the Sun wall. Take a photo from E. Do the same at marks 30, 60 and 90.
flow.parent: The bare half must face the wall squarely, not point at E and not point at the paper sign. At mark 0 the photo should show only sock. At mark 90 the edge of the sock should look like a straight line down the middle. With no phone, your child lies on the floor at E with one eye level with the ball. They hold the ruler at arm's length and measure how wide the ball and the bare part look.
flow.context: This is the first measuring step of How Much of the Moon Is Lit. You photograph the half-covered ball from the Earth spot at 0, 30, 60 and 90 degrees from the Sun.

flow.do: 1. Photograph the ball at marks 120, 150 and 180 in the same way. 2. Open each photo and make it bigger on the screen. 3. Hold the ruler across the middle of the ball. Measure the whole width and the width of the bare part. 4. Divide the bare width by the whole width and multiply by 100. Write the percent in the table.
flow.say: Now the Moon is on the far side of the Earth from the Sun. How much of the bare half can you see? Measure each photo, and work out the percent that is lit.
flow.kid: Photograph the ball at marks 120, 150 and 180. On each photo, measure the whole ball. Measure the bare part. Divide and multiply by 100.

ask.q: Did the lit part grow by the same amount at every step?
good: No. From 0 to 30 it grew very little, and from 60 to 90 it grew a lot.
The middle steps added about 25 percent each. The first and last steps added only about 7.

flow.parent: Expect about 0, 7, 25, 50, 75, 93 and 100 percent. Results within 5 of these are good. At mark 180 your own head is not in the way, because no lamp is used. If mark 30 gives more than 15 percent, check the ball. The bare half must face the wall, not E.
flow.context: This is the second measuring step of How Much of the Moon Is Lit. You finish the photos at 120, 150 and 180 degrees, and work out the percent lit on all seven.

flow.do: 1. Draw a graph with degrees from the Sun along the bottom and percent lit up the side. Plot the seven points and join them. 2. Compare the graph with the guesses. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 4. Then give the explanation in the parent note.
flow.say: Look at the shape of your line. Where is it steep, and where is it nearly flat? Now tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Draw a graph of your seven results. Where is the line steep? Where is it nearly flat? Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Why is so little of the face lit at mark 30?
good: The bare half is turned almost completely away from me, so I see only its edge.
I am looking at the lit half from behind and a little to the side.

flow.parent: After your child has explained, tell them this. Near Amavasya the lit half is turned almost fully away from us. So a big step shows only a thin edge. Near the half Moon each step turns a wide strip into view. The real Moon moves about 12 degrees further from the Sun each day. So it reaches mark 30 in about 2 and a half days. It reaches mark 90 in about 7 and a half days, and mark 180 in about 15 days.

check.q: The Moon is 60 degrees from the Sun, one-third of the way to full. About how much of its face is lit?
check.why: At 60 degrees about 25 parts in 100 are lit. Choosing one-third means expecting the lit part to grow evenly. It grows slowly at first, because we see the lit half almost from behind.

flow.context: This is the last step of How Much of the Moon Is Lit. You graph the percent lit at seven places, compare it with your guesses and explain the shape of the line.

experiments.title: The Shadow That Runs Out: where does the dark shadow of a seed end?
experiments.context: In this experiment you hold seeds of different sizes above white paper under one round bulb. You lift each seed until the dark middle of the shadow vanishes, and you measure that height. Then you look for a rule that fits every seed.
experiments.question: A seed is lifted above paper under a lamp. At what height does the dark middle of its shadow vanish? How does that height change when the seed is wider, and when the lamp is further away?
experiments.predict: Guess first. A chana is nearly twice as wide as a peppercorn. Will its dark shadow end at the same height, or higher, or lower? How many times as high? Then guess what happens when the paper is moved further from the lamp. Why do you think so? Write both guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bulb and switch off every other light. Keep the paper in the same place for all four things. Measure each height twice, because the moment the dark middle vanishes is hard to judge. Change only one thing at a time: first the width of the seed, then the distance of the paper from the lamp.
results_table: Height where the dark middle vanished, try 1 (mm)

materials.item: a room with one bare round bulb, on the ceiling or high on a wall. A round emergency lamp also works. A tube light does not
mustard seeds, black peppercorns and whole chana
a small shirt button without a rim, about 1 cm wide
thin sticks from a coconut broom, or toothpicks
a small lump of dough or a little sticky tape, to fix each thing to the end of a stick
white paper and a hardback book to rest it on
a ruler marked in millimetres, and a measuring tape
a table, and a clear patch of floor under the same bulb

experiments.safety: Measure the bulb only when it is switched off and cool. A grown-up measures a bulb that is high up. In the sunlight step, look only at the paper. Never look at the Sun.

schedule.what: At night, measure four small things and the bulb. Guess. Lift each thing over the paper on the table and measure where its dark shadow ends. Repeat on the floor. Find the rule. On a sunny day, try one seed in sunlight.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the four things on the table, and for two of them on the floor. Write the rule you found. Last, write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results, on a table 180 cm below a bulb 6 cm wide
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Here the bulb's distance divided by its width is 180 ÷ 6 = 30. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Ten peppercorns touching in a straight row along a ruler, the row reaching from 0 to 5 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Line up 10 seeds along the ruler. Divide the length of the row by 10 to get the width of one seed.

setup.art: A peppercorn fixed with a dab of dough to the tip of a thin broom stick, held level just above white paper under a ceiling bulb, with a small sharp dark shadow on the paper.
setup.caption: 2. Fix each thing to the end of a thin stick. Hold it just above the paper. The shadow is small and dark.

setup.art: The same peppercorn lifted higher above the paper: the shadow now has a small dark middle and a wide pale grey ring.
setup.caption: 3. Lift it slowly. The dark middle shrinks and a pale ring grows round it.

setup.art: The peppercorn held higher still beside an upright ruler, the shadow now only a faint pale smudge with no dark middle, and a second hand pointing to the height on the ruler.
setup.caption: 4. Stop when the dark middle vanishes. Measure the height above the paper.

flow.do: 1. Line up 10 mustard seeds, touching, along the ruler. Divide the length of the row by 10. Do the same for peppercorns and chana. Measure the button across. 2. Fix one of each to the tip of a thin stick with a dab of dough. 3. With the bulb off and cool, a grown-up measures the width of its glowing part. 4. Put white paper on a book on the table. Measure from the bulb to the paper.
flow.say: We need the width of each small thing in millimetres. One mustard seed is too small to measure. So we measure ten in a row and divide by ten.
flow.kid: Line up 10 seeds along the ruler. Divide the row's length by 10. Fix one of each on a stick. Measure the bulb and its distance.
flow.parent: A mustard seed is about 2 mm wide, a peppercorn about 5 mm, and a chana about 8 mm. Most round LED bulbs glow across about 6 cm. If the bulb is on a wall, tilt the book so the paper faces the bulb. Then the shadow of a seed is round and not stretched.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Shadow That Runs Out. Here you measure four small things, the bulb and the bulb's distance from the paper.

flow.do: 1. Switch off all other lights. 2. Hold the peppercorn just above the paper and show the small dark shadow. 3. Ask what will happen to the shadow as the peppercorn is lifted. 4. Ask how the chana's shadow will differ. Write the guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: The chana is nearly twice as wide as the peppercorn. When we lift them, will their dark shadows end at the same height? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the dark shadow under the peppercorn. What will happen when you lift it? Will the chana's shadow end higher or lower? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The shadow will get bigger and paler as I lift the seed.
The chana is wider, so the chana's dark shadow will last longer.
Both will end at the same height, because the lamp is the same. (A fair guess. The test will check it.)

flow.context: This step of The Shadow That Runs Out is for guessing. You guess how the dark shadow of a seed changes as the seed is lifted, and how a wider seed differs.

flow.do: 1. Stand the ruler upright on the paper. 2. Hold the mustard seed on the stick beside the ruler, just above the paper. Lift the seed slowly. 3. Stop when the dark middle of the shadow shrinks to nothing. Read the height on the ruler. 4. Do it again, then do the same for the peppercorn, the chana and the button. 5. Work out the mean height for each. Divide it by the width.
flow.say: Lift the seed very slowly and watch the dark middle of the shadow. The dark middle gets smaller and smaller. Tell me the moment it is gone. What is left on the paper then?
flow.kid: Lift the seed slowly beside the ruler. Watch the dark middle shrink. Stop when it vanishes. Read the height. Do it twice for each thing.

ask.q: What do you notice when you divide each height by the width?
good: The answer is nearly the same number for all four things.
A thing twice as wide has a dark shadow twice as long.

flow.parent: A second person reads the ruler while your child watches the shadow. The stick has a thin shadow too. Ignore it. Take a bulb 6 cm wide and 180 cm away. Expect about 6 cm for the mustard seed and 15 cm for the peppercorn. Expect about 24 cm for the chana and 36 cm for the button. Most people stop a little early, so a ratio from 25 to 32 is good for this lamp.
flow.context: This is the main step of The Shadow That Runs Out. You lift a mustard seed, a peppercorn, a chana and a button, and measure the height where each dark shadow ends.

flow.do: 1. Move the paper and the book to the floor under the same bulb. 2. Measure from the bulb to the paper again. 3. Repeat the test with the peppercorn and the chana, twice each. 4. Divide each mean height by the width, as before.
flow.say: Now the paper is further from the lamp. Will the dark shadows end at the same heights as before? Measure them and see.
flow.kid: Put the paper on the floor. Measure the distance to the bulb. Test the peppercorn and the chana again. Divide each height by the width.

ask.q: What changed when the paper was further from the lamp?
good: The dark shadows were longer.
The number I got by dividing was bigger, and again the same for both seeds.

flow.parent: With the floor 260 cm from the bulb, expect about 22 cm for the peppercorn. Expect about 35 cm for the chana. That gives about 43 for both. If you have no table under the bulb, use a chair seat and the floor.
flow.context: This step of The Shadow That Runs Out changes the distance. You move the paper from the table to the floor and test the peppercorn and the chana again.

flow.do: 1. Divide the distance from the bulb to the table by the width of the bulb. 2. Compare the answer with the numbers in the table. 3. Do the same for the floor. 4. Ask your child to say the rule. 5. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. Then read the parent note aloud.
flow.say: Divide the lamp's distance by the lamp's width. Compare that number with the number you got by dividing each height by each width. What do you notice? Then tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Divide the lamp's distance by the lamp's width. Compare it with your table. Say the rule. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: What rule joins the lamp and the dark shadow?
good: The dark shadow is as many seed-widths long as the lamp is lamp-widths away.
A wider lamp or a nearer lamp makes a shorter dark shadow.

flow.parent: For a bulb 6 cm wide, 180 cm from the paper, 180 ÷ 6 = 30. The dark shadow of every small thing ends about 30 widths behind it. After your child has explained, tell them this. The Sun is about 108 Sun-widths away from us. So in sunlight every dark shadow ends about 108 widths behind the thing. The Moon is 3,474 km wide. Its dark shadow ends about 375,000 km behind it, and the Earth is about that far from the Moon.

check.q: In sunlight a dark shadow ends about 108 widths behind a thing. Where does a 5 mm peppercorn's dark shadow end?
check.why: 5 mm times 108 is 540 mm, which is 54 cm. Choosing 'it never ends' means thinking of a shadow as a flat patch that only grows. The dark middle narrows to a point, because the Sun is wider than the peppercorn.

flow.context: This step of The Shadow That Runs Out finds the rule. You compare the lamp's distance divided by its width with the numbers you measured for each seed.

flow.do: 1. On a sunny day, find a patch of direct sunlight indoors or on a balcony. 2. Hold the paper so that it faces the Sun. 3. Hold the peppercorn on the stick in front of the paper, and move the stick slowly away. 4. Measure the distance from the peppercorn to the paper when the dark middle vanishes. Divide by the peppercorn's width.
flow.say: Never look at the Sun. How far does the peppercorn's dark shadow reach in sunlight?
flow.kid: Do this on a sunny day. Keep your back to the Sun. Look only at the paper. Move the peppercorn away until the dark middle vanishes. Measure.
flow.wait: Do this on a day when direct sunlight comes into your home or onto your balcony
flow.parent: Expect about 45 to 55 cm for a peppercorn, which gives a number near 100. The true value is 108. That number is the Sun's distance divided by the Sun's width. If no direct sunlight reaches your home, skip this step and use the number 108.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Shadow That Runs Out, for a sunny day. You measure where a peppercorn's dark shadow ends in sunlight.

experiments.title: A Black Card in the Dark: can a black card look white?
experiments.context: In this experiment you light a black card with a torch in a dark room, so that nothing else is lit. People who have not seen the card say what colour it looks. Then you add a white strip, and ask again. You will find out why the Moon looks white at night, although its ground is dark.
experiments.question: A black card is the only lit thing in a dark room. What colour does it look? Does the answer change when a white strip is put into the same light?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the black card is the only lit thing in the room, will people call it black, grey or white? What will they say when a white strip comes into the same light? Why do you think so? Write both guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same torch at the same distance all the time. Keep the room dark, so that no light falls on anything except the card. Ask each viewer alone, so that one answer does not lead the next. Only the neighbours of the card change: first nothing, then a white strip.
results_table: Black card with the white strip

materials.item: a piece of matt black chart paper or black card, about 15 cm square
a strip of white paper, about 4 cm by 15 cm
a piece of newspaper with small print and no pictures, about 15 cm square, glued to card
a torch or a phone torch
a sheet of paper rolled into a tube about 3 cm wide and 20 cm long, with tape
thread and tape, or a clothes peg, to hang the card
a dark room at night, with a doorway or an open space behind the card
family members or friends who have not seen the card

schedule.what: At night, hang the black card and aim a narrow torch beam at it. Guess. Ask viewers what colour the card is, alone and then with a white strip. Repeat with newspaper. Explain.

experiments.record: Write each viewer's words in the table. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Black card with the white strip
example_chart.note: These answers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your viewers will use their own words.

setup.art: A black card hanging by a thread in an open doorway, with a dark room behind it.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the black card in a doorway, with only a dark room behind it.

setup.art: A torch on a chair with a paper tube taped round its front, sending a narrow beam that lights only the hanging black card.
setup.caption: 2. Tape a paper tube to the torch. Aim it so that the whole spot of light lands on the card.

setup.art: The lit black card looking pale in the dark, and a hand sliding a white strip in front of its lower half, which makes the card above look black.
setup.caption: 3. Ask what colour the card looks. Then slide a white strip into the light, and ask again.

flow.do: 1. Hang the black card by a thread in an open doorway. Behind it there must be only a dark room or a far wall. 2. Tape the paper tube round the front of the torch. 3. Rest the torch on a chair about 50 cm from the card. 4. Switch off the room lights and switch on the torch. Move the torch until the whole spot of light lands on the card.
flow.say: We want the black card to be the only lit thing in the room. No light must spill past it. Check the wall behind. Is it dark?
flow.kid: Hang the black card in a doorway. Tape the tube to the torch. Aim the torch at the card. No light must spill past the card.
flow.parent: The test works only if nothing else is lit. If light spills past the card, move the torch closer or use a larger card. The viewers should wait in another room, so they do not see the card in ordinary light.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Black Card in the Dark. Here you hang a black card and aim a narrow torch beam so that only the card is lit.

flow.do: 1. Switch the torch off. 2. Ask your child what colour the viewers will say the card is. 3. Ask what they will say when a white strip is added. 4. Write both guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: The card is black. In a moment it will be the only thing lit in this room. What colour will people say it is? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what colour people will say the card is. Say why. Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Black, because the card is black. (A fair guess. The test will check it.)
Grey, because the torch makes it brighter.
It might look light, because there is nothing to compare it with.

flow.context: This step of A Black Card in the Dark is for guessing. You guess what colour a black card looks when it is the only lit thing in a dark room.

flow.do: 1. Bring in one viewer in the dark and seat them 2 metres from the card. 2. Switch on the torch. Ask what colour the card is. Write down their exact words. 3. Slide the white strip in front of the lower part of the card, inside the light. Ask again what colour the card is. 4. Take the strip away. Repeat with each viewer, one at a time.
flow.say: What colour is this card? Now look again. I have put a strip in front of it. What colour is the card now?
flow.kid: Bring in one viewer. Switch on the torch. Ask what colour the card is. Slide in the white strip. Ask again. Write down both answers.

ask.q: What happened to the card when the white strip came in?
good: It went from pale grey to black in a moment.
The card did not change, but it looked much darker.

flow.parent: Alone in the beam, the black card usually looks pale grey, silvery or even white. With the white strip in the same light, it looks black or dark grey at once. Your child knows the card is black, so it may look darker to them than to the viewers. That is a result too. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the main step of A Black Card in the Dark. A viewer says what colour the lit black card looks, first alone and then with a white strip beside it.

flow.do: 1. Take down the black card and hang the newspaper card in its place. 2. Ask each viewer what colour it is. 3. Slide the white strip into the light and ask again.
flow.say: Now we try a sheet of newspaper in the same way. What colour does it look by itself? And what colour does it look with the white strip in front?
flow.kid: Hang the newspaper card instead. Ask what colour it is. Slide in the white strip. Ask again.
flow.parent: Newspaper alone usually looks white. Beside white paper it looks grey. Printed newspaper reflects about half of the light that falls on it.
flow.context: This step of A Black Card in the Dark repeats the test with a newspaper card. Earlier a black card looked pale when it was the only lit thing.

flow.do: 1. Switch on the room lights. Show the viewers the black card. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Then read the parent note aloud.
flow.say: Here is the card in ordinary light. Now tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Switch on the lights. Show everyone the card. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Why did the black card look pale when it was alone?
good: It was the brightest thing we could see, so our eyes called it light.
There was nothing whiter to compare it with.

flow.parent: After your child has explained, tell them this. Our eyes judge how light a thing is by comparing it with its neighbours. The Moon's ground is dark grey. It reflects about 12 parts in every 100 of the sunlight that falls on it. An old tar road reflects about the same. In a black night sky it is the brightest thing in view, so it looks white.

check.q: The Moon reflects about 12 parts in 100 of the sunlight on it. Why does it look white at night?
options: It makes extra light of its own
Nothing brighter is near it in the dark sky
Its ground is as white as paper
check.why: The eye judges lightness by comparing neighbours, as the black card showed. Choosing 'as white as paper' takes the look for the fact. White paper reflects about 80 parts in 100, and the Moon only about 12.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Black Card in the Dark. You show the viewers that the card was black all along, and explain what you found.

activities.title: The Coin Eclipse: can a coin hide a steel plate?
activities.context: This activity starts the unit. You hide a round steel plate behind a small coin held near your eye. Then you move the coin a little, and a ring of plate appears. It shows how the small Moon can cover the huge Sun.

materials.item: a round steel plate or lid about 25 cm wide. A round wall clock also works
a coin, such as a 2-rupee or 5-rupee coin
a ruler and a measuring tape
a helper to measure

activities.record: Write the width of the plate and of the coin, and the two distances from your eye. Draw what you saw when the coin was near, exactly right, and a little too far, or tell your grown-up what you saw.

setup.art: A steel plate propped upright on a shelf, and a child standing three metres away with one eye closed, holding a coin in front of the open eye.
setup.caption: 1. Prop the plate upright. Stand 3 metres away. Close one eye and hold the coin in front of the other.

setup.art: Three small views side by side: a coin covering a plate completely, a coin exactly matching the plate's edge, and a coin with a thin ring of plate showing round it.
setup.caption: 2. Move the coin until it just covers the plate. Then move it a little further from your eye.

flow.do: 1. Prop the plate upright on a shelf or table, at the height of your child's eyes. 2. Measure 3 metres from the plate and mark the spot. 3. Give your child the coin. Ask if the coin can hide the whole plate, and how.
flow.say: The plate is about ten times as wide as this coin. Can the coin hide the whole plate from you? How? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hold the coin in front of you and look at the plate. Try to hide all of the plate.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Yes, if I hold the coin close to my eye.
A near thing looks bigger than a far thing.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Coin Eclipse. Here you guess whether a small coin can hide a steel plate ten times as wide.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands on the mark, closes one eye and holds the coin in front of the open eye. 2. They move the coin nearer and further until its edge just meets the edge of the plate. 3. The helper measures from the eye to the coin. 4. Divide the plate's width by the coin's width. Divide the plate's distance by the coin's distance.
flow.say: Move the coin until it only just covers the plate. Hold still while I measure. Now divide the two widths, and divide the two distances.
flow.kid: Close one eye. Move the coin until it just covers the plate. Hold still. Your helper measures from your eye to the coin.

ask.q: What do you notice about the two answers?
good: They are nearly the same number.
The plate is ten times as wide and ten times as far, so they look the same size.

flow.parent: Take a plate 25 cm wide and a coin 2.5 cm wide. The coin then sits about 30 cm from the eye. Both divisions give about 10. Take care that the ruler does not come near the open eye.
flow.context: This step of The Coin Eclipse measures the match. A coin held near your eye just covers a steel plate 3 metres away, and you compare the widths and the distances.

flow.do: 1. From the matching place, your child moves the coin about 5 cm further from the eye. 2. Ask what they see round the coin. 3. Then they bring the coin 5 cm nearer than the matching place. Ask again.
flow.say: Move the coin a little further from your eye. What do you see round its edge? Now bring it nearer. What happens to the ring?
flow.kid: Move the coin a little further away and look round its edge. Then bring it nearer.

ask.q: What changed when the coin was a little further from your eye?
good: A ring of plate showed all round the coin.
The coin looked smaller, so it could not cover the plate.

flow.context: This step of The Coin Eclipse changes the coin's distance. The coin just covered the plate, and now you move it a little further and a little nearer.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child the numbers for the Sun and the Moon. The Sun is about 400 times as wide as the Moon. It is about 390 times as far away. 2. Say that the Moon's distance changes by a few parts in 100 during each month. 3. Ask what people will see when a far Moon passes in front of the Sun.
flow.say: The Sun is about 400 times as wide as the Moon, and about 390 times as far away. The Moon is sometimes nearer and sometimes further. What will a far Moon leave showing?
flow.kid: Think about the coin held a little too far. What was left showing round it?
