flow.parent: A near Moon covers the whole Sun, and the eclipse is total. A far Moon leaves a ring of Sun, and the eclipse is annular. Remind your child that this is done with a plate. Nobody should ever try it with the real Sun.

check.q: The Moon passes exactly in front of the Sun while it is far from the Earth. What do people on the centre line see?
options: A ring of Sun round a black Moon
check.why: A far Moon looks a little smaller than the Sun, so a ring is left, as with the coin held too far. Choosing 'completely covered' forgets that the Moon's distance changes.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Coin Eclipse. A coin near your eye hid a plate, and a coin a little further away left a ring. Now you use that for the Sun and the Moon.

activities.title: Fit the Earth's Shadow: how wide is the Earth, in Moons?
activities.context: In this activity you use a photograph of a partial lunar eclipse. The curved dark edge on the Moon is the edge of the Earth's shadow. You find a round lid that fits the curve, and work out how wide the Earth is compared with the Moon.

materials.item: a photograph of a partial lunar eclipse, on a phone, a tablet or a printed page. Search for the words partial lunar eclipse photo
round things of different sizes: a bangle, a tumbler, a katori, jar lids and a small plate
a ruler
paper and a pencil

activities.record: Write the width of the Moon in the photo and the width of the round thing that fitted the shadow's edge. Write your working, and how many Moons wide the Earth came out.

setup.art: A phone lying flat showing a photo of the Moon with a curved dark shadow covering part of it, and a child holding a steel tumbler rim over the screen to match the curve.
setup.caption: 1. Lay round things over the photo. Find the rim that follows the curved dark edge best.

setup.art: A ruler measuring across the rim of a tumbler, next to a note that says Moon 3 cm, rim 8 cm.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the rim and the Moon. Divide the rim's width by the Moon's width.

flow.do: 1. Open a photograph of a partial lunar eclipse. 2. Ask your child what the dark part is, and what shape its edge has. 3. Ask if the edge belongs to a circle bigger or smaller than the Moon. Ask for a guess of how many Moons wide that circle is.
flow.say: The dark part is the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon. Look at its edge. Is it straight or curved? If you finished the curve into a full circle, how big would it be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the curved edge of the dark part. Guess how many Moons wide the full circle would be.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The edge is curved, but less sharply than the Moon's own edge. So the circle is bigger than the Moon.
The Earth is bigger than the Moon, so its shadow should be bigger.

flow.parent: Choose a photo where the shadow covers between a third and two-thirds of the Moon. The edge of the shadow is always a little blurred.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fit the Earth's Shadow. Here you look at a photograph of a partial lunar eclipse and guess the size of the Earth's shadow.

flow.do: 1. Make the photo bigger or smaller until the Moon is 3 cm wide on the screen. 2. Hold each round thing flat over the photo. Slide it until its rim lies along the curved dark edge. 3. Choose the rim that follows the curve best. Measure its width. 4. Divide that width by 3.
flow.say: Try each rim along the dark edge. Which one follows the curve best? Is the bangle too tight a curve? Is the plate too flat?
flow.kid: Make the Moon 3 cm wide. Try each rim along the dark edge. Pick the best fit. Measure it. Divide by 3.

ask.q: How many Moons wide is the shadow?
good: Between 2 and 3 Moons wide.
About two and a half times as wide as the Moon.

flow.parent: The true answer is about 2.6 Moons, so a rim about 8 cm wide fits a 3 cm Moon. The edge is blurred, so any answer from 2 to 3 and a half is good. Aristarchus himself got 2.
flow.context: This is the main step of Fit the Earth's Shadow. You find a round rim that follows the curved edge of the Earth's shadow in the photograph, and compare its width with the Moon's.

flow.do: 1. Remind your child of The Shadow That Runs Out. There every dark shadow grew narrower with distance, and then ended. 2. Say that the Earth's shadow narrows in the same way. By the time it reaches the Moon, it has lost about one Moon-width. 3. Ask your child to add 1 to their answer. That is the Earth's width in Moons.
flow.say: In The Shadow That Runs Out, each dark shadow got narrower as it went. The Earth's shadow has lost about one Moon-width by the time it reaches the Moon. So how wide is the Earth itself?
flow.kid: The Earth's shadow gets narrower on its way to the Moon. It loses about one Moon-width. Add 1 to your answer. That is the Earth's width.
flow.parent: In sunlight a dark shadow loses one width of itself for every 108 widths of distance. The Moon is about 110 Moon-widths from the Earth. So the Earth's shadow is about one Moon-width narrower there than the Earth. About 2.6 plus 1 gives 3.6 Moons.
flow.context: This step of Fit the Earth's Shadow corrects for the shadow's narrowing. You found the Earth's shadow to be about 2 to 3 Moons wide where it crosses the Moon.

flow.do: 1. Give the real widths. The Earth is 12,742 km wide and the Moon is 3,474 km wide. 2. Ask your child to divide. 3. Compare the answer with their own result. 4. Ask what the round edge of the shadow says about the Earth's shape.
flow.say: Divide the Earth's real width by the Moon's real width. How close was your answer? You measured the Earth with a tumbler and a photograph.
flow.kid: The Earth is 12,742 km wide. The Moon is 3,474 km wide. Divide. How close was your answer?
flow.parent: 12,742 ÷ 3,474 is about 3.7. The shadow's edge is round in every lunar eclipse, whichever way the Earth is turned. Only a ball makes a round shadow from every side.

check.q: The edge of the Earth's shadow on the Moon is curved in every lunar eclipse. What does this show?
check.why: Only a ball throws a round shadow from every direction. A flat disc would sometimes throw a thin, stretched shadow. Aristotle used this reasoning about 2,400 years ago.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fit the Earth's Shadow. You compare your result, found from the curve of the Earth's shadow, with the real widths of the Earth and the Moon.

activities.title: Eclipse Detective: find the pattern in 12 real eclipses
activities.context: In this activity you study a list of every eclipse of 2024, 2025 and 2026. You look for a pattern in the dates and the kinds, and you use it to predict the first eclipse of 2027.

materials.item: a wall calendar or a phone calendar that shows 2024 to 2027
paper and a pencil
two colour pencils

activities.record: Copy the list of 12 eclipses. Write the gap in days between each eclipse and the next. Write the two patterns you found, and your prediction for early 2027.

setup.art: A handwritten list of twelve dates on a notebook page, with some marked in yellow for solar and some in blue for lunar, and brackets joining them into pairs.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the 12 eclipses. Colour the solar ones and the lunar ones differently.

setup.art: A child counting days on a wall calendar with a finger, and writing the number 177 between two pairs of dates.
setup.caption: 2. Count the days between the eclipses. Look for numbers that repeat.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the list of 12 eclipses. 2. Ask them to copy it, with solar eclipses in one colour and lunar eclipses in another. 3. Ask what they notice before they count anything.
flow.say: Here is every eclipse of three years. Copy the list. Colour the solar and lunar ones differently. What do you notice straight away?
flow.kid: Copy the list of 12 eclipses. Colour the solar ones and the lunar ones differently.

ask.q: What do you notice?
good: They come in pairs, close together.
Each pair has one solar and one lunar eclipse.
There are long gaps with no eclipses.

chart.title: Every eclipse of 2024, 2025 and 2026 (dates by world time)

flow.context: This is the first step of Eclipse Detective. Here you copy a list of the 12 eclipses of 2024, 2025 and 2026, and look at it before counting.

flow.do: 1. Use the calendar to count the days between the two eclipses of each pair. 2. Count the days from the first eclipse of each pair to the first eclipse of the next pair. 3. Write every gap beside the list.
flow.say: Count the days inside each pair. Then count from one pair to the next. Which numbers keep coming back?
flow.kid: Count the days inside each pair. Then count from one pair to the next pair. Write every gap.

ask.q: Which numbers keep coming back?
good: About 14 or 15 days inside a pair.
About 177 days from one pair to the next.

flow.parent: Inside the pairs the gaps are 14, 14, 15, 14, 14 and 16 days. That is half a Moon month, from Purnima to Amavasya or back. Now count from the first eclipse of one pair to the first of the next. The gaps are 177, 177, 177, 163 and 176 days. The gap of 163 days is from 7 September 2025 to 17 February 2026. There the solar eclipse came first, so that pair began half a Moon month early. Count lunar to lunar or solar to solar. Then every gap is 176 to 178 days, except one of 149 days.
flow.context: This step of Eclipse Detective counts the gaps. The 12 eclipses of 2024 to 2026 come in six pairs, and you count the days inside and between the pairs.

flow.do: 1. Ask why the pairs are half a Moon month apart. 2. Ask why the pairs come about 177 days apart. 3. Give the reasons in the parent note after your child has tried.
flow.say: A solar eclipse needs Amavasya, and a lunar eclipse needs Purnima. How far apart are those? And why might the pairs come about every six months?
flow.kid: A Moon month is about 30 days. How many days are there from Amavasya to Purnima?

ask.q: Why do the pairs come about six months apart?
good: The Moon's path crosses the Earth's path at two points. The Sun lines up with one of them about every six months.
Eclipses can happen only in those weeks.

flow.parent: The Moon's path is tilted about 5 degrees. The Sun lines up with one of the two crossing points, the nodes, about every 173 days. Six Moon months are 177 days, which is the nearest whole number of Moon months. Sometimes the gap is five Moon months, or 148 days, to catch up.
flow.context: This step of Eclipse Detective explains the gaps. You found that eclipses come in pairs about two weeks apart, and that the pairs come about 177 days apart.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to predict the first eclipse of 2027 from the solar eclipse of 12 August 2026. 2. They add 177 days on the calendar. 3. Tell them the real date and kind. 4. Ask what kind should come two weeks later.
flow.say: Start from the solar eclipse of the twelfth of August 2026. Add 177 days. What date do you reach? What kind of eclipse do you expect two weeks after that?
flow.kid: Start at 12 August 2026. Count 177 days on the calendar. Write the date you reach.
flow.parent: Adding 177 days to 12 August 2026 gives 5 February 2027. The real eclipse is an annular solar eclipse on 6 February 2027. A penumbral lunar eclipse follows on 20 February 2027. Your child has predicted an eclipse to within a day, with a calendar and a pencil.

check.q: A lunar eclipse happens tonight. When is a solar eclipse most likely?
options: About two weeks before or after
check.why: The Sun stays near a node for about five weeks. So the Amavasya two weeks before or after an eclipse Purnima is also near the node. Choosing 'one year later' forgets that the seasons come about 19 days earlier each year.

flow.context: This is the last step of Eclipse Detective. You use the gap of 177 days between pairs of eclipses to predict the first eclipse of 2027.

activities.title: Aristarchus's Angle: how a small mistake moved the Sun
activities.context: In this activity you draw the triangle that Aristarchus used to find the Sun's distance, on the floor. You try four angles, and see how a tiny change in the angle moves the Sun a very long way.

materials.item: a protractor
a string about 4 metres long
a ruler and a measuring tape
chalk, or paper slips and sticky tape
a sheet of paper, and a clear floor about 3.5 metres long

activities.record: Make a table with three columns. Write the angle at the Earth, and the distance from the Moon to the Sun in centimetres. Write how many times the Earth-to-Moon distance that is.

setup.art: A sheet of paper on the floor with two dots 5 centimetres apart labelled E and M, and a long straight line of tape running from M at a right angle to the line EM.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the Earth E and the Moon M 5 cm apart. Make a long line from M at a right angle. The Sun is somewhere on it.

setup.art: A protractor centred on E and a string stretched from E across the floor at a steep angle, crossing the long line far from M.
setup.caption: 2. Stretch a string from E at 80, 85, 87 and 89 degrees. Mark where it crosses the Sun line.

flow.do: 1. Tape the paper to the floor at one end of the clear space. Mark two dots 5 cm apart. Label them E for the Earth and M for the Moon. 2. Use the protractor to draw a line from M at a right angle to the line EM. 3. Continue this line along the floor with the tape measure or chalk, for 3 metres.
flow.say: At an exact half Moon, the Sun's light hits the Moon from the side. So the corner at the Moon is a right angle. The Sun is somewhere along this long line. How could we find where?
flow.kid: Mark the Earth and the Moon 5 cm apart. Draw a line from the Moon at a right angle. The Sun is somewhere on that line.

ask.q: How could we find where the Sun is on the line?
good: Measure the angle between the Moon and the Sun, seen from the Earth.
Draw a line from the Earth towards the Sun and see where the two lines cross.

flow.context: This is the first step of Aristarchus's Angle. Here you mark the Earth and the Moon on the floor. You also mark the line on which the Sun must lie at an exact half Moon.

flow.do: 1. Put the centre of the protractor on E, with its zero line along EM. 2. Hold one end of the string on E. Stretch it across the 80 degree mark until it crosses the Sun line. Mark the crossing. 3. Measure from M to the crossing. 4. Do the same for 85, 87 and 89 degrees.
flow.say: Stretch the string from the Earth at eighty degrees. Where does it cross the Sun line? Now try eighty-five, eighty-seven and eighty-nine. Guess each crossing before you stretch the string.
flow.kid: Stretch the string from E at 80 degrees. Mark where it crosses the Sun line. Measure from M. Then try 85, 87 and 89 degrees.

ask.q: What happens to the crossing as the angle gets close to 90 degrees?
good: It races away. Two more degrees triple the distance.
At 90 degrees the lines would never meet.

flow.parent: Expect about 28 cm at 80 degrees and 57 cm at 85 degrees. Expect about 95 cm at 87 degrees and 286 cm at 89 degrees. A small protractor cannot set 89 degrees exactly. Any answer from 2 to 4 metres is fine, and that wide spread is the point of the activity.
flow.context: This is the main step of Aristarchus's Angle. You stretch a string from the Earth at four angles and measure where each one meets the Sun's line.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to divide each distance by 5. The answers show how many times as far the Sun is as the Moon. 2. Tell them Aristarchus measured 87 degrees. 3. Tell them the true angle is 89.85 degrees. On this floor the Sun would be about 19 metres away.
flow.say: Divide each crossing distance by 5. In our drawing the Moon is 5 centimetres from the Earth, so this gives the Sun's distance in Moon-distances. Aristarchus measured 87 degrees, so he said the Sun is 19 times as far as the Moon. The true angle is 89.85 degrees. Where is the Sun then?
flow.kid: Divide each distance by 5. Aristarchus measured 87 degrees. What did he get? The true angle is 89.85 degrees.
flow.parent: The answers are about 6, 11, 19 and 57 times. At 89.85 degrees the answer is about 380 times, close to the real figure of about 390. On the floor that is about 19 metres, which is longer than most flats.
flow.context: This step of Aristarchus's Angle turns the floor distances into numbers. Strings from the Earth at 80, 85, 87 and 89 degrees crossed the Sun's line further and further away.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to try to mark 89.85 degrees on the protractor. 2. Ask why Aristarchus could not have measured it. 3. Ask whether his method was wrong.
flow.say: Try to find 89.85 degrees on your protractor. Can you tell it from 90? Was Aristarchus's method wrong, or was it his measurement?
flow.kid: Try to find 89.85 degrees on the protractor. Can you tell it from 90? Was the method wrong, or the measurement?

ask.q: Was the method wrong, or the measurement?
good: The method was right. The angle was too close to 90 degrees to measure by eye.
He also could not tell the exact moment of the half Moon.

check.q: Aristarchus's angle was wrong by less than 3 degrees. How wrong was his distance to the Sun?
check.why: He got 19 times the Moon's distance, and the real figure is about 390. Near 90 degrees, a tiny change in the angle makes a huge change in the distance. Choosing '3 parts in 100' expects a small error to stay small.

flow.context: This is the last step of Aristarchus's Angle. You found that a change from 87 to 89 degrees triples the Sun's distance, and now you judge Aristarchus's result.

activities.title: Swap Places: the Earth seen from the Moon
activities.context: In this activity the half-covered ball from How Much of the Moon Is Lit becomes the Earth. You look at it from the Moon's places on the floor. You find out what an astronaut on the Moon sees during our phases and our eclipses.

materials.item: the ball half covered by a dark sock, and the tumbler, from How Much of the Moon Is Lit
the floor marks E, 0, 90 and 180 from that experiment, or four new marks
paper and colour pencils

activities.record: For our Amavasya, our half Moon and our Purnima, write one word for the Earth as the astronaut sees it: full, half or dark. Then say what the astronaut sees during a total lunar eclipse.

setup.art: The half-covered ball on an upturned tumbler at the floor mark E, its bare half facing the wall with the SUN sign, and a child lying on the floor at mark 0 looking back at the ball.
setup.caption: 1. Put the ball on mark E as the Earth, with its bare half facing the Sun wall. Look at it from mark 0.

setup.art: A child's drawing of three Earths in a row: a full round Earth, a half Earth and a dark Earth with a thin red ring round it.
setup.caption: 2. Look from marks 0, 90 and 180. Say how much of the Earth is lit from each.

flow.do: 1. Stand the ball on the tumbler at mark E. It is now the Earth. Turn its bare half to face the Sun wall. 2. Ask your child what the Moon looks like from the Earth when the Moon is at mark 0. 3. Ask what the Earth will look like from the Moon at that moment.
flow.say: In How Much of the Moon Is Lit, the ball at mark 0 showed no lit part. That was Amavasya. Now the ball is the Earth. What will an astronaut at mark 0 see? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The ball is now the Earth. Stand it on the tumbler at mark E. Turn its bare half to the Sun wall.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The astronaut is on the Sun's side, so they look at the Earth's lit half.
It will be a full Earth.

flow.context: This is the first step of Swap Places. The half-covered ball from How Much of the Moon Is Lit is now the Earth, and you guess how it looks from the Moon.

flow.do: 1. Your child lies at mark 0 with one eye level with the ball and looks back at it. 2. They do the same from mark 90 and from mark 180. 3. They point to the lit part of the Earth from each mark and say how much it is.
flow.say: Look back at the Earth from each mark. How much of it is lit? Compare that with what the Moon looked like from the Earth at the same mark.
flow.kid: Look at the Earth ball from marks 0, 90 and 180. Point to the lit part each time.

ask.q: How do the Earth's phases compare with the Moon's?
good: They are opposite. When we have no Moon, the astronaut has a full Earth.
The two lit shares add up to 100 percent.

flow.parent: From mark 0 your child sees the whole bare half, a full Earth. From mark 90 they see half. From mark 180 they see only the sock. A full Earth lights the Moon's night side. We see that light as earthshine, the faint glow on the dark part of a thin crescent Moon.
flow.context: This is the main step of Swap Places. You look at the Earth ball from three of the Moon's places and draw what an astronaut would see.

flow.do: 1. Ask what the astronaut sees during our total lunar eclipse, when the Moon is at mark 180 exactly in line. 2. Ask what the astronaut sees during our total solar eclipse, at mark 0 exactly in line. 3. Your child shows both with the ball, and says what they see. Then read the parent note.
flow.say: During our lunar eclipse, the Earth stands between the astronaut and the Sun. What does the astronaut see? During our solar eclipse, the astronaut looks at a full Earth. What is different about it?
flow.kid: Say what the astronaut sees at mark 180, when the Earth hides the Sun. Say what is dark on the Earth at mark 0.
flow.parent: In our lunar eclipse the astronaut sees the black Earth cover the Sun. The Earth looks nearly four times as wide as the Sun from there. A thin red ring of air glows all round the Earth. In our solar eclipse the astronaut sees a full Earth with one small dark spot moving across it. The spot is the Moon's shadow, at most about 270 km wide on an Earth 12,742 km wide.

check.q: It is Purnima on the Earth. What does the Earth look like from the Moon?
options: A dark Earth, with no lit part showing
check.why: At Purnima the Moon is on the side of the Earth away from the Sun. From there you look at the Earth's night side. Choosing 'a full Earth' forgets that the two sets of phases are opposite.

flow.context: This is the last step of Swap Places. You saw that the Earth's phases from the Moon are the opposite of the Moon's. Now you work out how our eclipses look from there.

games.title: Place the Moon: where is the Moon on its path?
games.context: This is a clue card game with a small board. The board shows the Earth, the direction of sunlight and eight places on the Moon's path. Each card says what someone sees. You put the Moon on the right place, and say why.

printables.title: The board: the Earth, the sunlight and 8 places for the Moon
items: Draw the Earth as a small circle in the middle of a page.
On the left edge, draw arrows pointing right. Write: sunlight comes from here.
Draw a big circle round the Earth for the Moon's path. Mark 8 places on it, evenly spaced.
Place 1 is on the left, between the Earth and the Sun: Amavasya, 0 degrees from the Sun.
Number the places 2 to 8 going round anticlockwise. That is down from place 1, then right, then up.
Place 3 is at the bottom: the growing half Moon, 90 degrees from the Sun.
Place 5 is on the right, on the far side of the Earth from the Sun: Purnima, 180 degrees.
Place 7 is at the top: the shrinking half Moon.
Places 2 and 8 are crescents. Places 4 and 6 are more than half lit.

printables.title: 24 clue cards: a clue on the front, the place and the reason on the back. Print on both sides

items.f: No Moon is seen all night. It is Amavasya.
items.b: Place 1. The Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, and its lit half faces away from us.

items.f: A thin crescent is low in the west, just after sunset.
items.b: Place 2. The Moon is a little way past the Sun, so it sets soon after the Sun.

items.f: A half Moon is high in the sky at sunset. It sets near midnight.
items.b: Place 3. The Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun, a quarter of the way round.

items.f: The Moon is more than half lit. It is already up in the east in the afternoon.
items.b: Place 4. The Moon is between the half Moon and Purnima, in Shukla Paksha.

items.f: The Moon rises in the east as the Sun sets in the west. It is Purnima.
items.b: Place 5. The Moon is opposite the Sun, 180 degrees away.

items.f: The Moon is more than half lit. It rises about three hours after sunset.
items.b: Place 6. The Moon is a few days past Purnima, in Krishna Paksha.

items.f: A half Moon rises near midnight. It is high in the sky at sunrise.
items.b: Place 7. The Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun again, on the other side.

items.f: A thin crescent is low in the east, just before sunrise.
items.b: Place 8. The Moon is close to the Sun again, and rises just before it.

items.f: About 15 parts in 100 of the Moon's face are lit, and the lit part is growing.
items.b: Place 2. At 45 degrees from the Sun, about 15 parts in 100 are lit.

items.f: Exactly half of the Moon's face is lit. Tomorrow more will be lit.
items.b: Place 3. This is the growing half Moon, in the middle of Shukla Paksha.

items.f: About 85 parts in 100 of the Moon's face are lit. Tomorrow less will be lit.
items.b: Place 6. At 135 degrees from the Sun about 85 parts in 100 are lit, and the Moon is shrinking.

items.f: The Moon's shadow crosses the Earth. People in a narrow strip see the Sun completely covered.
items.b: Place 1, exactly on the line. This is a total solar eclipse, and the Moon is near the Earth.

items.f: The full Moon turns dark red for an hour.
items.b: Place 5, exactly on the line. This is a total lunar eclipse, and the Moon is inside the Earth's shadow.

items.f: A bright ring of Sun shows round a black Moon.
items.b: Place 1, exactly on the line. This is an annular eclipse, and the Moon is far from the Earth.

items.f: The sea has its biggest tides of the month. There are two answers.
items.b: Places 1 and 5. At Amavasya and Purnima the Sun and the Moon pull along one line.

items.f: The sea has its smallest tides of the month. There are two answers.
items.b: Places 3 and 7. At the half Moons the Sun and the Moon pull at right angles.

items.f: It is the middle of Shukla Paksha, the fortnight when the Moon grows.
items.b: Place 3. About a week after Amavasya the Moon is a half Moon.

items.f: It is the middle of Krishna Paksha, the fortnight when the Moon shrinks.
items.b: Place 7. About a week after Purnima the Moon is a half Moon again.

items.f: The dark part of a thin crescent glows faintly with earthshine. There are two answers.
items.b: Places 2 and 8. From the Moon the Earth is nearly full then, and it lights the Moon's night side.

items.f: An astronaut on the Moon sees a full Earth.
items.b: Place 1. The astronaut is on the Sun's side of the Earth and looks at its day side.

items.f: An astronaut on the Moon sees the Earth as a crescent. There are two answers.
items.b: Places 4 and 6. The Earth's phases are the opposite of the Moon's.

items.f: It is the night of Diwali.
items.b: Place 1. Diwali falls on Amavasya.

items.f: It is the evening of Karthigai Deepam, or of Buddha Purnima.
items.b: Place 5. Both festivals fall on a Purnima.

items.f: People look for the thin crescent that begins a new month of the Islamic calendar.
items.b: Place 2. The first thin crescent after Amavasya shows in the west after sunset.

printables.title: Score sheet: one row for each card, two points for each card

rules: Draw the board. Use a coin or a button as the Moon. Shuffle the 24 cards and put them clue side up in a pile.
Read the top card aloud. Do not turn it over.
Each player in turn puts the Moon on a place and gives a reason. The reason must say where the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are.
Turn the card over. The right place earns 1 point. A reason that matches the back earns 1 more point.
For a card with two answers, you need both places for the point.
With friends, take turns to go first. The player with the most points after the whole pile wins.
Playing alone? Go through the whole pile. A score of 30 out of 48 is good, and 40 is very good. Then play again and try to beat your score.

setup.art: A hand-drawn board on a page: a small Earth in the middle, arrows of sunlight from the left, and eight numbered places on a circle round the Earth.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the board. Number the eight places.

setup.art: A pile of clue cards beside the board, and a child holding a button over place 3 on the Moon's path.
setup.caption: 2. Read a clue. Put the Moon on the place you think is right. Say why.

setup.art: A card turned over to show the words Place 3 and a reason, with a child ticking a score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score a point for the place and a point for the reason.

flow.do: 1. Draw the board together, following the nine lines of the board printable. 2. Put the button on place 1 and ask where the Moon's lit half is facing. 3. Move it to place 5 and ask again. 4. Cut out the cards.
flow.say: Sunlight comes from the left. So the left half of the Moon is always the lit half. From the Earth in the middle, how much of that half can you see at each place?
flow.kid: Draw the board. Sunlight comes from the left. The Moon's left half is always lit. Cut out the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Place the Moon. You draw a board with the Earth, the sunlight and eight places for the Moon, and get the cards ready.

flow.do: Play by the rules. Read each clue, place the Moon, give the reason, then turn the card over and score. Stop at any card the players got wrong, and move the Moon to the right place together.
flow.say: Read the clue. Where must the Moon be for someone to see that? Put it there and tell me why. Then we check.
flow.kid: Read a clue. Put the Moon on a place. Say why. Turn the card over. Score your points.

ask.q: What told you where the Moon was?
good: The time it rose or set.
How much of it was lit, and whether it was growing.
An eclipse needs the Moon exactly on the line at place 1 or place 5.

flow.parent: The cards about rising and setting are the hardest. A Moon at place 3 trails the Sun by a quarter of a day. So it sets about six hours after sunset. A Moon at place 7 is a quarter of a day ahead of the Sun.
flow.context: In this step of Place the Moon you play the card game. For each clue you put the Moon on its path round the Earth and give a reason.

flow.do: 1. Pick out the cards that fooled you. 2. Say which word in the clue should have helped. 3. Ask your child which card surprised them most.
flow.say: Which cards fooled you? Where did you put the Moon? Which word in the clue points to the right place?
flow.kid: Find a card that fooled you. Which word in the clue should have helped?

check.q: A thin crescent Moon is seen low in the east before sunrise. Is the lit part growing or shrinking?
check.why: A crescent before sunrise is at place 8, a few days before Amavasya, so it is shrinking. A growing crescent is seen in the west after sunset. Choosing 'growing' treats every crescent as a new one.

flow.context: This is the last step of Place the Moon. You look again at the clue cards that fooled you, and say why.

games.title: Total, Ring, Part or Miss? An eclipse card game
games.context: This is a card game about which eclipse happens. Each card gives the Moon's phase and its distance from the ground. It also says how close the Moon is to the straight line through the Sun and the Earth. You say which eclipse people see, if any.

printables.title: The rule card: read it before every game
items: A solar eclipse needs Amavasya. A lunar eclipse needs Purnima. At any other phase there is no eclipse.
Amavasya, on the line, Moon nearer than 375,000 km: total solar eclipse. The dark shadow reaches the ground.
Amavasya, on the line, Moon further than 375,000 km: ring eclipse. The dark shadow ends above the ground.
Amavasya, a little off the line: partial solar eclipse. Only the pale outer shadow touches the Earth.
Purnima, on the line: total lunar eclipse, whatever the Moon's distance.
Purnima, a little off the line: partial lunar eclipse.
Far off the line: no eclipse. This is what happens in most months.

printables.title: 20 situation cards: the situation on the front, the eclipse and the reason on the back. Print on both sides

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is exactly on the line. It is 352,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Total solar eclipse. The dark shadow is about 375,000 km long, so it reaches the ground with 23,000 km to spare.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is exactly on the line. It is 399,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Ring eclipse. The dark shadow ends about 24,000 km above the ground.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is exactly on the line. It is 368,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Total solar eclipse. The dark shadow reaches the ground with 7,000 km to spare.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is exactly on the line. It is 381,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Ring eclipse. The dark shadow ends about 6,000 km above the ground.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is exactly on the line. It is 373,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Total solar eclipse, but only just. The dark spot on the ground is very small, and totality lasts a few seconds.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is exactly on the line. It is 377,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Ring eclipse, but only just. The ring of Sun is very thin.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is exactly on the line. It is 360,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Total solar eclipse. The Moon is near, so the dark spot is wide and totality is long.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is a little off the line. It is 355,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Partial solar eclipse. A near Moon does not help if the dark shadow misses the Earth.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is a little off the line. It is 397,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Partial solar eclipse. Only the pale outer shadow touches the Earth.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is far above the line. It is 362,000 km from the ground.
items.b: No eclipse. The Moon's shadow passes above the Earth.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is far below the line. It is 390,000 km from the ground.
items.b: No eclipse. The Moon's shadow passes below the Earth.

items.f: Amavasya. The Moon is far above the line. It is 400,000 km from the ground.
items.b: No eclipse. This is what happens at most Amavasyas.

items.f: Purnima. The Moon is exactly on the line. It is 399,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Total lunar eclipse. The Earth's dark shadow is about 1.4 million km long and about 9,200 km wide at the Moon. Distance does not matter here.

items.f: Purnima. The Moon is exactly on the line. It is 352,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Total lunar eclipse. The whole Moon is inside the Earth's dark shadow, and it turns red.

items.f: Purnima. The Moon is a little off the line. It is 370,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Partial lunar eclipse. Part of the Moon stays outside the dark shadow.

items.f: Purnima. The Moon is a little off the line. It is 395,000 km from the ground.
items.b: Partial lunar eclipse. A curved dark edge covers part of the Moon.

items.f: Purnima. The Moon is far above the line. It is 365,000 km from the ground.
items.b: No eclipse. The Moon passes above the Earth's shadow.

items.f: Purnima. The Moon is far below the line. It is 388,000 km from the ground.
items.b: No eclipse. This is what happens at most Purnimas.

items.f: Purnima. The Moon is far below the line. It is 398,000 km from the ground.
items.b: No eclipse. The Moon passes below the Earth's shadow.

items.f: A half Moon. The Moon is exactly on the line of the Earth's path. It is 375,000 km from the ground.
items.b: No eclipse. At a half Moon the Sun, the Earth and the Moon make a right angle, and no shadow can fall on anything.

printables.title: Score sheet: one row for each card, two points for each card
items: My answer: total solar, ring, partial solar, total lunar, partial lunar or none (1 point)

rules: Read the rule card aloud. Shuffle the 20 cards and put them situation side up in a pile.
Read the top card aloud. Do not turn it over.
Every player writes which eclipse people see, or writes none. Every player also writes a short reason.
For a solar eclipse on the line, compare the Moon's distance with 375,000 km, the length of the dark shadow.
Turn the card over. The right eclipse earns 1 point. A reason that matches the back earns 1 more point.
The player with the most points after 20 cards wins.
Playing alone? Go through the whole pile. A score of 28 out of 40 is good, and 35 is very good. Then play again and try to beat your score.

setup.art: A printed rule card with seven lines beside a pile of situation cards, on a table with two pencils and score sheets.
setup.caption: 1. Read the rule card. Put the 20 cards in a pile, situation side up.

setup.art: A child writing the words ring eclipse on a score sheet while another child reads a card aloud.
setup.caption: 2. Read a situation. Write which eclipse happens, and why.

setup.art: A card turned over to show the words Total solar eclipse and a reason, with a child ticking a score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score a point for the eclipse and a point for the reason.

flow.do: 1. Read the seven lines of the rule card aloud. 2. Remind your child of The Shadow That Runs Out. There each dark shadow ended at a fixed length. 3. Say that the Moon's dark shadow is about 375,000 km long. 4. Cut out the cards and give each player a score sheet.
flow.say: In The Shadow That Runs Out, every dark shadow had an end. The Moon's dark shadow ends about 375,000 kilometres behind it. If the ground is further away than that, what do people see?
flow.kid: The Moon's dark shadow is about 375,000 km long. Think about what happens if the ground is further away. Cut out the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Total, Ring, Part or Miss. You read the rule card, which uses the length of the Moon's dark shadow, and get the cards ready.

flow.do: Play by the rules. Read each card, write the eclipse and the reason, then turn the card over and score. Talk about any card that the players got wrong.
flow.say: Read the card. Is it Amavasya or Purnima? Is the Moon on the line? Then look at the distance. Write your answer and your reason.
flow.kid: Read a card. Write which eclipse happens. Write why. Turn the card over. Score your points.

ask.q: For which cards did the Moon's distance matter?
good: Only for a solar eclipse exactly on the line.
For a lunar eclipse the distance never mattered, because the Earth's shadow is so long and wide.

flow.parent: Seven of the 20 cards have no eclipse. In real life the share is far higher. A year has 12 or 13 Amavasyas, and only 2 or 3 of them bring any solar eclipse.
flow.context: In this step of Total, Ring, Part or Miss you play the card game. For each situation you say which eclipse people see, or that there is none.

flow.do: 1. Sort the cards into six piles by their answers. 2. Count each pile. 3. Ask which single fact decides between a total eclipse and a ring.
flow.say: Sort the cards by their answers. Which pile is biggest? What one fact decides between a total eclipse and a ring?
flow.kid: Sort the cards by their answers. Which pile is biggest? What decides between total and ring?

check.q: At Purnima the Moon is exactly on the line, and it is at its furthest from the Earth. What happens?
options: A ring eclipse of the Moon
check.why: The Earth's dark shadow is about 1.4 million km long, far longer than any distance of the Moon. So the Moon's distance does not matter. Choosing 'a ring eclipse' carries the rule for solar eclipses over to lunar ones.

flow.context: This is the last step of Total, Ring, Part or Miss. You sort the situation cards by the eclipse each one gives, and say what decides it.

projects.title: The Angle Diary: does the real Moon follow your graph?
projects.context: In this project you watch the real Moon on five evenings. Each evening you measure its angle from the place where the Sun has just set, and judge how much of its face is lit. Then you compare the real Moon with your graph from How Much of the Moon Is Lit.

materials.item: a place with a view of the western sky: a terrace, a balcony or a west-facing window
a notebook and a pencil
your graph from How Much of the Moon Is Lit, or the angle rule from this lesson
a wall calendar that marks Amavasya

projects.safety: Never look at the Sun. Start each evening only after the Sun has gone below the horizon or behind the buildings.

schedule.what: Three days after Amavasya, just after sunset: find out how many degrees your fist covers. Measure the Moon's angle from the sunset point. Draw the Moon and judge the percent lit.
Two evenings later: measure the angle, draw the Moon and judge the percent lit.
Two evenings later again: measure, draw and judge.
Two evenings later again: measure, draw and judge.
Two evenings later again: measure, draw and judge. Then plot your five points on the graph and compare.

projects.record: Keep a table with the date, the days since Amavasya, and the angle in fists and in degrees. Add a photo or drawing of the Moon and the percent lit that you judged. Plot the five points on your graph of percent lit against degrees.

setup.art: A child on a terrace just after sunset with one arm stretched out and the fist closed, lined up with the glow on the western horizon.
setup.caption: 1. After sunset, hold your fist at arm's length. Start at the place where the Sun went down.

setup.art: The same child stepping the fist across the sky towards a crescent Moon, with faint outlines of four fists in a row between the horizon glow and the Moon.
setup.caption: 2. Step your fist across the sky to the Moon. Count the fists.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of dates, fists, degrees, small Moon drawings and percents, beside a graph with five points plotted near a smooth curve.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the Moon and judge the percent lit. After five evenings, plot the points on your graph.

flow.do: Day 1, three days after Amavasya, just after sunset. 1. Hold your fist at arm's length. Count how many fists fit from the horizon to straight overhead. 2. Divide 90 by that number. That is the number of degrees one fist covers. 3. Find the Moon. Step your fist from the sunset point to the Moon and count. 4. Take a photo of the Moon, or draw it. Judge the percent lit.
flow.say: First we find out how big your fist is against the sky. Horizon to overhead is ninety degrees. Then we count fists from where the Sun went down to the Moon. How much of the Moon looks lit?
flow.kid: Wait until the Sun has set. Count fists from the horizon to overhead. Divide 90 by that number. Then count fists from the sunset point to the Moon.

ask.q: From your graph, how much of the Moon should be lit at this angle?
good: At about 35 degrees, about 10 percent.
A thin crescent.

flow.parent: Most people count 9 fists from the horizon to overhead, so one fist covers about 10 degrees. Three days after Amavasya the Moon is about 35 degrees from the Sun. It shows a thin crescent, about 10 percent lit. If clouds hide the Moon, read its angle from the Sun in a free sky program such as Stellarium Web. Carry on the next clear evening.
flow.context: This is day 1 of The Angle Diary. You find how many degrees your fist covers, then measure how far the real Moon is from the place where the Sun has set.

flow.do: Days 2, 3 and 4. Each visit is two evenings after the one before. 1. Go out just after sunset. 2. Count the fists from the sunset point to the Moon. Change the fists to degrees. 3. Take a photo of the Moon, or draw it. Judge the percent lit: about 10, 25, 50, 75 or 90. 4. Before you look, use your graph to predict the percent from the angle.
flow.say: How far has the Moon moved from the Sun in two days? Use your graph to predict how much will be lit. Then look and see.
flow.kid: Go out after sunset. Count fists from the sunset point to the Moon. Predict the percent lit from your graph. Then look, and photograph or draw the Moon.
flow.wait: Do this every second evening for about a week

ask.q: How many degrees did the Moon move in two days?
good: About 24 degrees, a little over two fists.
About 12 degrees a day.

flow.parent: Expect about 60 degrees and 25 percent on day 5 after Amavasya. Expect about 85 degrees and nearly 50 percent on day 7. Expect about 110 degrees and about 65 percent on day 9. Measuring ten or more fists across the sky is rough. An error of one fist is normal.
flow.context: These are days 2, 3 and 4 of The Angle Diary. On each evening you measure the Moon's angle from the sunset point and compare the lit part with your prediction.

flow.do: Day 5, two evenings after day 4. 1. Measure, predict, photograph or draw, and judge once more. 2. Plot all five evenings as points on the graph from How Much of the Moon Is Lit. 3. Ask your child how well the real Moon follows the line. 4. Ask what could explain the points that are off the line.
flow.say: Plot your five evenings on the graph. Do the points follow the line from the sock Moon? Where they do not, what might be the reason?
flow.kid: Plot your five evenings on your graph. Do the points follow the line? Say why some might be off.
flow.wait: Do this two evenings after the fourth evening

ask.q: What might explain a point that is off the line?
good: My fist is a rough ruler, and I may have miscounted.
Judging the percent lit by eye is hard.
I measured from the sunset point, but the Sun had already moved a little below the horizon.

flow.parent: The points should rise slowly at first and then faster, like the line from the sock Moon. Around Purnima the Moon is too far from the sunset point to measure well with fists. That is why the diary stops about 11 days after Amavasya.
flow.context: This is the last day of The Angle Diary. You plot five evenings of the real Moon on your graph from How Much of the Moon Is Lit. Then you judge how well they match.

challenges.title: An Eclipse Machine: the smallest disc that hides the lamp
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In The Shadow That Runs Out, the dark shadow of each seed got narrower with distance and then ended. Here you use that rule to design a disc that keeps a target in full shadow.
challenges.problem: Engineers who study the Sun's corona make their own eclipses with a disc. Your target is a circle 1 cm wide, drawn on paper. A paper disc must hang 20 cm in front of it, between the target and the lamp. Find the smallest disc that keeps the whole target inside the dark middle of the shadow.
constraints: Use the same bulb and the same table as in The Shadow That Runs Out.
The disc must be 20 cm from the paper.
No part of the target may be in the pale ring of the shadow.
Work out the size first, then cut discs and test.
materials: thin card, scissors and a ruler
thin sticks from a coconut broom and sticky tape
white paper with a circle 1 cm wide drawn on it
your numbers from The Shadow That Runs Out
general: Cut a disc much bigger than the target, and trim it until the dark middle just covers the target.
Use your number from The Shadow That Runs Out to work out how much width the dark middle loses in 20 cm.
Cut discs of 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.1 cm, and test them in order.
creative: Move the paper further from the lamp, so that every dark shadow is longer and a smaller disc works.
Cover part of the bulb with a card that has a small hole, so that the lamp is narrower.
Try the same design in sunlight, where the dark middle loses only 1 cm in every 108 cm.
challenges.your_turn: Now set your own target and distance. Work out the disc first, and then test it. Write down how close your sum was to the disc that really worked.

setup.art: A small paper disc on a thin stick held 20 centimetres above a sheet of paper with a small drawn circle, under a ceiling bulb, with the disc's shadow falling on the circle.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a disc 20 cm above the target. Look at the dark middle of its shadow.

setup.art: Four paper discs of different sizes on sticks laid in a row beside a ruler, with their widths written beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Work out the smallest disc that should work. Cut several sizes and test them.

flow.do: 1. Remind your child of The Shadow That Runs Out. With a bulb 6 cm wide and 180 cm away, every dark shadow ended 30 widths behind the seed. 2. Read the problem and the four constraints together. 3. Ask how much narrower the dark middle becomes in 20 cm.
flow.say: In The Shadow That Runs Out, a thing one centimetre wide had a dark shadow about thirty centimetres long. So the dark middle lost one centimetre of width in thirty centimetres. How much does it lose in twenty?
flow.kid: Your dark shadow lost 1 cm of width in about 30 cm. How much does it lose in 20 cm? Use your own number.
flow.parent: Use your child's own number from the experiment. If it was 30, the dark middle loses 20 ÷ 30 of a centimetre, which is about 0.7 cm. The target is 1 cm wide. So the disc must be at least about 1.7 cm wide.
flow.context: This is the first step of An Eclipse Machine. You use your result from The Shadow That Runs Out to work out how much a dark shadow narrows in 20 cm.

flow.do: 1. Cut card discs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.1 cm wide. Tape each to the tip of a thin stick. 2. Hold each disc 20 cm above the target, measured with the ruler. 3. Look at the shadow. Is the whole target inside the dark middle? 4. Write yes or no for each disc.
flow.say: Hold each disc exactly twenty centimetres above the target. Is the whole circle inside the dark middle, or does the pale ring touch it?
flow.kid: Cut four discs. Hold each one 20 cm above the target. Is the whole target in the dark middle? Write yes or no.
flow.parent: With a number near 30, the discs of 1.2 and 1.5 cm should fail. The disc of 1.8 cm should just pass. Keep the disc flat, facing the lamp. A tilted disc casts a narrower shadow.
flow.context: This is the main step of An Eclipse Machine. You test paper discs of four sizes, 20 cm above a target circle, to find the smallest one that keeps it in full shadow.

flow.do: 1. Compare the test with the sum. 2. Tell your child about the two spacecraft in the parent note. 3. Ask your child to work out the length of the dark shadow of their disc in sunlight.
flow.say: Did the smallest disc that worked match your sum? In space, engineers have done this with a disc 1.4 metres wide. How long is its dark shadow in sunlight?
flow.kid: Did your sum match the test? A disc in space is 1.4 metres wide. Multiply by 108.

ask.q: How long is the dark shadow of a disc 1.4 metres wide in sunlight?
good: 1.4 times 108 is about 151 metres.

flow.parent: Proba-3 is a pair of European spacecraft, launched from Sriharikota on an Indian PSLV rocket in December 2024. One carries a disc about 1.4 metres wide. The other flies about 150 metres behind it, just inside the tip of the dark shadow, and photographs the corona. India's Aditya-L1 does the same job with a small disc inside its own telescope.

check.q: A disc must keep a telescope in full shadow from further away. What must change?
check.why: The dark middle of a shadow gets narrower with distance. A longer distance needs a wider disc. Choosing 'nothing' treats a shadow as the same width all the way along.

flow.context: This is the last step of An Eclipse Machine. You compare your sum with the disc that really worked, and learn how spacecraft make their own eclipses.

challenges.title: A True-Scale Eclipse on a Stick (needs a sunny window, balcony or terrace)
challenges.context: This is a building challenge for a sunny day. You fix a ball for the Earth and a peppercorn for the Moon on a stick, at their true sizes and true distance apart. Then you try to make both kinds of eclipse with real sunlight.
challenges.problem: Build a model of the Earth and the Moon to one scale. Use real sunlight to make a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse with the model. Find out which is easier to make, and how carefully the stick must be aimed.
constraints: The Earth is a ball 2 cm wide. The Moon is about 5.5 mm wide. They are 60 cm apart.
Use only sunlight. No lamp or torch.
Never look at the Sun. Keep your back to the Sun and look only at the two balls.
Measure how far you can tip the stick before each eclipse ends.
materials: a straight stick or a strip of stiff card at least 70 cm long
stiff dough or clay for a ball 2 cm wide, and a black peppercorn about 5 mm wide
two toothpicks or pins, and sticky tape
general: Rest one end of the stick on a windowsill or a chair back, to keep it steady.
First aim the stick so that its own shadow is as short as it can be. Then make small changes.
Stand both balls on toothpicks of the same height, so that they are level with each other.
creative: Tape a small white card behind the Earth ball. It shows where the peppercorn's shadow falls when the aim is a little off.
Slide the peppercorn 5 cm nearer the Earth and 5 cm further away, and compare the two shadows on the Earth ball.
Tip the Moon's end of the stick up by 5 cm, to copy the tilt of the Moon's path, and see both eclipses fail.
challenges.your_turn: Now build a bigger model on the same scale, with an Earth 4 cm wide. Work out the size of the Moon and the length of the stick first. Say what the bigger model shows better.

setup.art: A long stick with a 2 centimetre dough ball on a toothpick at one end and a peppercorn on a toothpick 60 centimetres along, both at the same height.
setup.caption: 1. Fix the Earth ball and the peppercorn Moon on the stick, 60 cm apart.

setup.art: A child with their back to a sunny window holding the stick so that the peppercorn's tiny grey shadow falls on the dough ball.
setup.caption: 2. With your back to the Sun, aim the stick until the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth ball.

setup.art: The stick turned end for end, with the dough ball's wide dark shadow covering the peppercorn completely.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the stick round. Let the Earth's shadow cover the Moon.

flow.do: 1. Roll a ball of stiff dough 2 cm wide. Push it onto a toothpick and tape the toothpick upright at one end of the stick. 2. Fix the peppercorn to the tip of the second toothpick with a dab of dough. 3. Tape it upright 60 cm from the Earth ball, at the same height. 4. Ask your child to check the scale with the real sizes.
flow.say: The Earth is 12,742 kilometres wide and our ball is two centimetres. The Moon is 3,474 kilometres wide and 384,400 kilometres away. Check my sizes. Are they right for this scale?
flow.kid: Fix a 2 cm ball at one end of the stick. Fix the peppercorn 60 cm away. Check the scale with the real sizes.
flow.parent: The Moon is 3,474 ÷ 12,742 of the Earth's width, which is 0.27. So the model Moon is 5.5 mm wide. The distance is about 30 Earth-widths, which is 60 cm. A peppercorn of 5 to 6 mm is close enough.
flow.context: This is the first step of A True-Scale Eclipse on a Stick. You build the Earth and the Moon on a stick, with one scale for their sizes and their distance.

flow.do: 1. Stand with your back to the Sun, in direct sunlight. 2. Hold the stick with the Moon end towards the Sun. Aim it until the peppercorn's shadow falls on the Earth ball. 3. Look at the shadow on the ball. Is there a dark dot, or only a grey smudge? 4. Tip the stick slowly until the shadow leaves the ball. Measure how far the far end moved.
flow.say: Keep your back to the Sun. Look only at the Earth ball. Can you land the Moon's shadow on it? What does the shadow look like? How far can you tip the stick before it misses?
flow.kid: Keep your back to the Sun. Aim the stick. Land the Moon's shadow on the Earth ball.

ask.q: What does the Moon's shadow look like on the Earth ball?
good: A small grey smudge, with hardly any dark middle.
It is tiny, and it is hard to keep on the ball.

flow.parent: A peppercorn's dark shadow in sunlight is 54 to 65 cm long, depending on its width. So at 60 cm you get a pale smudge, or a dark dot smaller than a pinhead. That is true to life. The real dark shadow only just reaches the Earth. The shadow leaves the ball when the far end of the stick moves 1 to 2 cm.
flow.context: This is the solar eclipse step of A True-Scale Eclipse on a Stick. In real sunlight, you try to make the peppercorn Moon's shadow fall on the Earth ball 60 cm away.

flow.do: 1. Turn the stick end for end, so that the Earth ball is towards the Sun. 2. Aim it until the Earth ball's shadow covers the peppercorn. 3. Tip the stick slowly until the peppercorn comes out of the dark shadow. Measure how far the far end moved. 4. Ask your child which eclipse was easier to make, and why.
flow.say: Now let the Earth's shadow fall on the Moon. How much of the peppercorn is covered? Which eclipse was easier to make? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Turn the stick round. Let the Earth's shadow cover the peppercorn.

ask.q: Which eclipse was easier to make, and why?
good: The lunar eclipse. The Earth's dark shadow is much wider than the Moon.
For the solar eclipse the dark dot is tiny, so the aim must be nearly perfect.

flow.parent: At 60 cm the Earth ball's dark shadow is about 1.4 cm wide, about 2.6 times the peppercorn. So the whole Moon goes dark, and it stays dark while the stick tips a little. The real Moon's path is tilted 5 degrees. On this model that lifts the Moon about 5 cm above the line, far enough for both shadows to miss.

check.q: On a true-scale model, why is a lunar eclipse easier to make than a solar eclipse?
options: The Moon is brighter than the Sun
The Earth's dark shadow is much wider than the Moon's
check.why: At the Moon's distance the Earth's dark shadow is about 2.6 Moons wide. The Moon's dark shadow has almost run out by the time it reaches the Earth. Choosing the other answers ignores the sizes of the two shadows.

flow.context: This is the lunar eclipse step of A True-Scale Eclipse on a Stick. Earlier the peppercorn Moon's shadow made only a tiny smudge on the Earth ball. Now the Earth ball shadows the Moon.

worksheets.title: Phases, moonlight and the two kinds of eclipse

items.p: Put these phases in order, starting from Amavasya.
items.why: After Amavasya the lit part grows through Shukla Paksha to Purnima. Then it shrinks through Krishna Paksha.

items.p: The fortnight from Amavasya to Purnima, when the lit part grows, is called ____ Paksha.
items.why: Shukla Paksha is the bright fortnight. Krishna Paksha is the dark fortnight, from Purnima back to Amavasya.

items.p: The Moon makes its own light.
items.why: False. The Moon only reflects sunlight. Its lit side always faces the Sun.

items.p: What causes the Moon's phases?
opts: The Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon
We see different shares of the lit half
Clouds hide part of the Moon
items.why: The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As the Moon goes round the Earth, we see more or less of that half. The Earth's shadow touches the Moon only in a lunar eclipse.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: The night when no Moon is seen
The night when the whole lit half is seen
The fortnight when the lit part shrinks
The dark middle of a shadow
The pale ring round the dark middle
items.why: These are the main words of the unit. The first three are about phases. The umbra and the penumbra are the two parts of a shadow. The corona shows only in a total solar eclipse.

items.p: Solar eclipse or lunar eclipse? Sort each line.
items: The Moon's shadow falls on the Earth
The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
It is seen from half the Earth
It is total only in a narrow strip
It is safe to watch with bare eyes
items.why: In a solar eclipse the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth. In a lunar eclipse the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. The Earth's shadow is on the Moon itself, so half the Earth can see it.

items.p: Some people think the Moon's phases are the Earth's shadow. Give one piece of evidence against this idea.
items.a: A crescent Moon is often seen close to the Sun in the sky. The Earth's shadow points away from the Sun, so it cannot fall there. Also, a half-covered ball shows every phase when only its place changes, with no shadow from anything.
items.why: A strong answer gives a fact that the shadow idea cannot explain. The best one is a crescent or a half Moon seen in the same part of the sky as the Sun.

items.p: Draw the Sun, the Earth and the Moon at Purnima. Shade the half of the Moon that is dark.
items.a: The three are in a line with the Earth in the middle. The half of the Moon facing the Sun and the Earth is left bright. The half facing away is shaded.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the Earth between the Sun and the Moon. It shades the far half of the Moon, so that the lit half faces both the Sun and the Earth.
items.art: A blank strip with a small Sun drawn at the left edge and space for the Earth and the Moon.

items.p: The Moon moves about 12 degrees further from the Sun each day. How many degrees is that after 5 days?
items.why: 12 times 5 is 60 degrees. At 60 degrees about a quarter of the Moon's face is lit.

items.p: The Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun. How much of its face is lit?
items.why: At 90 degrees we look at the Moon from the side. So we see half of the lit half and half of the dark half. That is a half Moon.

items.p: A lunar eclipse can be seen only from a narrow strip of the Earth.
items.why: False. The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon itself. Everyone on the night side of the Earth sees the same darkened Moon.

items.p: Label the parts of this picture of a solar eclipse.
labels: The place that sees a total eclipse
a: The Moon: the small ball between the Sun and the Earth
The umbra: the narrow dark cone behind the Moon
The penumbra: the wide pale cone round the umbra
The place that sees a total eclipse: the small spot where the umbra touches the Earth
items.why: The umbra is the dark middle of the Moon's shadow, and only its tip reaches the Earth. The penumbra is much wider, and people inside it see a partial eclipse.
items.art: The Sun on the left, the Moon in the middle and the Earth on the right, with a narrow dark cone and a wide pale cone behind the Moon, and four blank label lines.

items.p: The Moon's ground is dark grey. Why does the Moon look bright in the night sky?
opts: It is lit by city lights
Nothing brighter is near it in the sky
items.why: The eye judges how light a thing is by comparing it with its neighbours. The Moon reflects only about 12 parts in 100 of the sunlight on it, but the sky round it is black.

items.p: Which is the better eclipse to see: a total solar eclipse or a total lunar eclipse?

views.who: A person who travels to see solar eclipses
views.says: A total solar eclipse shows the corona and brings out stars in the daytime. Nothing else is like it, even though it lasts only a few minutes.

views.who: A grandmother who watches from her terrace
views.says: A lunar eclipse comes to my own terrace. It is safe for bare eyes, it lasts over an hour, and the whole family can watch together.
Each one teaches something different. The solar eclipse shows the Sun's outer layer. The lunar eclipse shows the Earth's shadow and the state of the Earth's air.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this lesson. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For the first: the corona shows only in totality. For the second: everyone on the night side of the Earth can see a lunar eclipse. For the third: the red colour of the eclipsed Moon comes from the Earth's air.
items.why: A strong answer uses a fact about how each eclipse works, and treats the other views fairly. There is no single right choice.

items.p: Three of these make their own light. Which one does not?
items.why: The Moon only reflects sunlight. The Sun, a firefly and a flame each make light.

items.p: The Moon is 30 degrees from the Sun. About how much of its face is lit?
items.why: At 30 degrees only about 7 parts in 100 are lit. Choosing 17 means expecting the lit part to grow evenly, by one-sixth at each of six steps.

items.p: The lit shares at 60 degrees and at 120 degrees add up to ____ parts in 100.
items.why: 25 and 75 add up to 100. The part that is lit at 60 degrees is the same size as the part that is dark at 120 degrees.

items.p: The lit part of the Moon grows fastest around the half Moon.
items.why: True. From 60 to 90 degrees the lit share rises from 25 to 50. From 0 to 30 degrees it rises only from 0 to 7.

items.p: Two days after Amavasya the Moon has moved 24 degrees. Why is so little of its face lit?
items.a: The lit half is still turned almost fully away from the Earth. We look at it nearly from behind, so we see only a thin edge of it.
items.why: A strong answer says which way the lit half faces, and where we look from. It does not say the Sun lights less of the Moon, because the Sun always lights half.

items.p: Under one lamp, dark shadows are 40 widths long. How many millimetres long is the dark shadow of a 3 mm bead?
items.why: The dark shadow is 40 bead-widths long. 3 times 40 is 120 mm, which is 12 cm.

items.p: The paper is moved twice as far from the same lamp. What happens to a seed's dark shadow?
opts: It becomes about twice as long
items.why: From further away the lamp looks narrower, so the dark middle of the shadow narrows more slowly. Twice the distance gives twice the length.

items.p: Where is each person standing during a solar eclipse?
items: A bite is missing from the Sun
The Sun looks like a crescent
It is an ordinary sunny day
items.why: In the umbra the whole Sun is covered. In the penumbra part of the Sun still shows. Outside both, nothing is covered.

items.p: Match each thing to the length of its dark shadow in sunlight.
items.why: In sunlight every dark shadow is about 108 widths long. 2 mm times 108 is 216 mm. 3,474 km times 108 is about 375,000 km.

items.p: Put these in order, from the narrowest to the widest.
items: The Moon's dark spot on the Earth
The Earth's dark shadow at the Moon
a: The Moon's dark spot on the Earth
The Earth's dark shadow at the Moon
items.why: The dark spot is at most about 270 km wide. The Moon is 3,474 km. The Earth's dark shadow at the Moon is about 9,200 km. The Earth is 12,742 km.

items.p: A far Moon looks smaller in the sky than a near Moon.
items.why: True. The Moon's distance changes from about 363,000 to about 405,000 km. A thing that is further away looks smaller.

items.p: A plate is 8 times as wide as a coin. Where must the coin be to just hide the plate?
opts: 8 times nearer the eye than the plate
items.why: Two things look the same size when their widths and their distances are in the same ratio. The coin is one-eighth as wide, so it must be one-eighth as far.

items.p: The Sun is about 400 times as wide as the Moon. Explain how the Moon can still cover it.
items.a: The Sun is also about 390 times as far away as the Moon. A thing that is 400 times as wide and about 400 times as far looks the same size. So the Moon can just cover the Sun.
items.why: A strong answer compares both the widths and the distances. It may add that the match is not exact, which is why some eclipses are rings.

items.p: Is a shadow a real thing?

views.says: A shadow is only a place the light does not reach. It has no weight and it cannot push anything. Only the light and the bodies are real.
The Moon's shadow has a length, a width, a speed and a path. I can work them out to the second. Anything I can measure and predict is real enough.
My bees stop flying when the Moon's shadow passes over the hives. Whatever changes what living beings do is real to them.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using something you measured. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For the first: when the lamp is switched off, the shadow is gone and nothing is left behind. For the second: the dark shadow of each seed had a length that could be measured. For the third: bees stopped flying during totality in 2017.
items.why: A strong answer says what 'real' means for that view, and uses a measurement or an observation. People still argue about this.

items.p: Draw the shadow of a ball lit by a wide lamp. Mark the umbra, the penumbra and the tip.
items.a: A wide lamp on one side and a smaller ball in the middle. Behind the ball a dark cone narrows to a point, which is the tip of the umbra. Round it a pale cone widens, which is the penumbra.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the umbra getting narrower and ending, and the penumbra getting wider. The lamp is drawn wider than the ball.
items.art: A wide round lamp at the left and a small ball in the middle of an empty box, with space to the right for the shadow.

items.p: Three of these happen only at Amavasya. Which one does not?
items.why: A lunar eclipse needs the Earth between the Sun and the Moon, which is Purnima. Every solar eclipse needs the Moon between the Sun and the Earth, which is Amavasya.

items.p: Why is there not a solar eclipse at every Amavasya?
opts: The Moon's path is tilted about 5 degrees
items.why: The tilt carries the Moon above or below the straight line at most Amavasyas, so its shadow misses the Earth. An eclipse needs Amavasya near a node.

items.p: Every eclipse season has both a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse.
items.why: True. The Sun stays near a node for about five weeks. That is long enough for one Amavasya and one Purnima to fall near the node.

items.p: Eclipse pairs come about 177 days apart. A Moon month is 29.5 days. How many Moon months is that?
items.why: 177 divided by 29.5 is 6. Eclipses need Amavasya or Purnima, so the gap between seasons is a whole number of Moon months.

items.p: Babylonian sky-watchers predicted eclipses from lists of dates. What could they not explain that you now can?
items.a: They knew when an eclipse was likely, from the pattern of dates. They could not say why eclipses come in pairs, or why a solar eclipse is total in one place and partial in another. Shadows, the tilt of the Moon's path and the Moon's distance explain these.
items.why: A strong answer separates knowing the pattern from knowing the cause. It names at least one thing that the shadow explanation adds.

items.p: After a big volcanic eruption, the eclipsed Moon looks much darker. What does this show?
opts: The Moon's light passed through the Earth's air
items.why: Dust high in the Earth's air blocks some of the sunlight that is bent into the shadow. So the eclipsed Moon is a report on the Earth's air.

items.p: Put the events of a total lunar eclipse in order.
items: The whole Moon turns dark red
The dark edge slides off the Moon
The Moon enters the pale penumbra
A curved dark edge crosses the Moon
a: The Moon enters the pale penumbra
A curved dark edge crosses the Moon
The whole Moon turns dark red
The dark edge slides off the Moon
items.why: The Moon meets the pale outer shadow first, then the edge of the umbra. Once it is wholly inside the umbra it is lit only by red light bent through the Earth's air.

items.p: Was Aristarchus's measurement of the Sun's distance good science?

views.says: Yes. He asked a question that measuring could answer, and his method was correct. The answer got better when the tools got better.
No. An answer that is 20 times too small is of no use. A method counts only when you can carry it out with the tools you have.
The most useful part is that he showed his working. Because of that, later people could find exactly where the error came from.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For the first: the same triangle gives the right answer with the true angle of 89.85 degrees. For the second: near 90 degrees a tiny error in the angle gives a huge error in the distance. For the third: his error was traced to one number, the angle of 87 degrees.
items.why: A strong answer uses the triangle and its numbers. It treats the other views fairly. Historians still disagree about how to judge early measurements.

items.p: In Aristarchus's triangle the angle at the Earth changes from 87 to 89 degrees. What happens to the Sun's distance?
opts: It becomes about three times as great
items.why: At 87 degrees the Sun is 19 times as far as the Moon. At 89 degrees it is 57 times as far. Close to 90 degrees, the two lines are almost side by side, so they meet very far away.

items.p: A half Moon gives half as much light as a full Moon.
items.why: False. A half Moon gives only about one-tenth as much. Sunlight strikes its rough ground from the side, and long shadows cover much of the lit part.

items.p: One town sees a total solar eclipse about once in 375 years. Lunar eclipses are seen often. Explain why.
items.a: The Moon's dark shadow has nearly ended when it reaches the Earth, so the dark spot is at most about 270 km wide. Only people in its narrow path see totality. The Earth's dark shadow is about 9,200 km wide at the Moon and covers it completely. Everyone on the night side of the Earth can see that.
items.why: A strong answer compares the sizes of the two shadows. It says where each shadow falls: on a small part of the Earth, or on the Moon itself.

items.p: Match each observation to what it showed.
pairs: The Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round
The shadow's curve is about 2.6 Moons wide
The Earth is nearly 4 Moons wide
Sunlight is bent through the Earth's air
A ring of Sun is left round the Moon
The Moon is far from the Earth
A pale glow shows round the covered Sun
The Sun has a faint outer layer
items.why: Each observation is evidence for one conclusion. The shadow is 2.6 Moons wide after losing about one Moon-width on the way. That gives about 3.6 Moons for the Earth, close to the real 3.7.

items.p: Draw what an astronaut on the Moon sees during our total lunar eclipse.
items.a: A black sky. A large black disc, the Earth, covers the Sun. A thin ring of red-orange light glows all the way round the Earth's edge. The ground of the Moon in front is dull red.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the Earth much wider than the hidden Sun, and a thin red ring of air round the Earth. That ring is the light of every sunrise and sunset on the Earth.
items.art: A strip of grey Moon ground along the bottom of a black sky, with the sky left empty.

items.p: The Earth's shadow, 2.6 Moons wide at the Moon, has narrowed by 1 Moon-width. How many Moons wide is the Earth?
items.why: 2.6 plus 1 is 3.6. The real figure is 12,742 divided by 3,474, which is about 3.7.

items.p: The two points where the Moon's path crosses the Earth's path are called ____.
items.why: Eclipses happen only when Amavasya or Purnima falls near a node. Indian astronomers named the two nodes Rahu and Ketu.

items.p: Safe or not safe for watching a partial solar eclipse?
items: Patches of light under a leafy tree
items.why: The safe ways either use a tested filter or do not look at the Sun at all. Sunglasses and X-ray film let through light that can burn the eye without any pain.

quiz.p: On which night is no Moon seen at all?
opts: The night of the half Moon
quiz.why: At Amavasya the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, and its lit half faces away from us.

quiz.p: At Purnima, where is the Earth?
opts: Between the Sun and the Moon
On the far side of the Sun
Between the Moon and the stars
quiz.why: At Purnima the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, so we look at the Moon's whole lit half. The three are usually not in an exact line, so there is no eclipse.

quiz.p: Which fact shows that the phases are not the Earth's shadow?
opts: A crescent Moon is seen near the Sun
quiz.why: The Earth's shadow points away from the Sun. A crescent Moon is close to the Sun in the sky, where that shadow cannot fall.

quiz.p: The Moon is 120 degrees from the Sun. About how much of its face is lit?
quiz.why: At 120 degrees about 75 parts in 100 are lit. Choosing two-thirds means expecting the lit part to grow evenly with the angle.

quiz.p: How much of the sunlight that falls on it does the Moon reflect?
quiz.why: The Moon's ground is dark grey, like an old tar road. It looks white only because the sky round it is black.

quiz.p: From inside the umbra of the Moon's shadow, what does the Sun look like?
quiz.why: The umbra is the part of the shadow where the whole Sun is covered. In the penumbra only part of the Sun is covered.

quiz.p: In sunlight, about how many widths behind a thing does its dark shadow end?
quiz.why: The Sun is about 108 Sun-widths away, so every dark shadow in sunlight is about 108 widths long. Choosing 'never' treats a shadow as a flat patch with no length.

quiz.p: A solar eclipse is exactly on the centre line. What decides whether it is total or a ring?
opts: The Moon's distance from the Earth
quiz.why: A near Moon looks big enough to cover the Sun, and its dark shadow reaches the ground. A far Moon leaves a ring.

quiz.p: Why does the Moon turn red in a total lunar eclipse?
opts: Sunlight bent through the Earth's air reaches it
quiz.why: The Earth's air bends a little sunlight into the shadow and scatters the blue out of it. The same thing reddens the Sun at sunrise and sunset.

quiz.p: Who can see a total lunar eclipse?
opts: Only people in a narrow strip
Everyone on the night side of the Earth
quiz.why: The Earth's shadow is on the Moon itself. Everyone who can see the Moon sees it darkened.

quiz.p: How often does an eclipse season come?
quiz.why: The Sun lines up with a node of the Moon's path about every 173 days. Choosing 18 years mixes this up with the saros, after which eclipses repeat.

quiz.p: Which is a safe way to watch a partial solar eclipse?
opts: With bare eyes for a few seconds
quiz.why: Only a tested solar filter is safe for looking at the Sun. The eye feels no pain while sunlight burns it, so a short look is not safe.

applications: Astronomers work out every eclipse years ahead, to the second. Their tables tell people where to stand to see one. Indian panchangams list the eclipses of the year in the same way.
A tithi is a day of the Indian Moon calendar. One tithi is the time the Moon takes to move 12 degrees further from the Sun. So festival dates come from the Moon's angle from the Sun.
Spacecraft that study the Sun carry a disc that hides the Sun's bright face, like a small Moon. India's Aditya-L1 watches the corona this way all the time.

Engineers who send landers to the Moon plan for lunar eclipses. For a lander on the Moon, our lunar eclipse is a solar eclipse. Its solar panels get no sunlight for hours, and the ground cools quickly.

Historians use old records of eclipses to fix the dates of kings and battles. The same records show that the Earth's spin is slowing. A day is now about 2 thousandths of a second longer than it was a hundred years ago.
Astronomers find planets round other stars by a kind of eclipse. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star's light dips a little, again and again.
A white roof reflects most of the sunlight that falls on it, and a dark roof takes most of it in. Some Indian cities paint roofs white so that the rooms below stay cooler.
