open_questions.q: Why is the Sun's corona so much hotter than its surface?
open_questions.why_open: The surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius and the corona is over a million. Waves and tiny flares are the two main ideas. Aditya-L1 and other spacecraft are measuring which matters more.

open_questions.q: How dark will the next total lunar eclipse be?
open_questions.why_open: The colour depends on dust and cloud in the Earth's air on that day. A volcano can erupt months before and change it. Nobody can say exactly in advance.

open_questions.q: What do other animals and plants sense during a solar eclipse?
open_questions.why_open: Bees stop flying, and some birds go to roost. Scientists do not yet know whether they answer only the fading light, or also the cooling air and the change in the wind.

open_questions.q: Exactly how fast is the Earth's spin slowing, and why does the rate change?
open_questions.why_open: Old eclipse records show a slowing that is not steady. Tides, melting ice and movements deep inside the Earth all play a part. Their shares are still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Did Thales really predict the eclipse of 585 BCE?
open_questions.why_open: The only account was written about 150 years later. No method known at the time could say where a solar eclipse would be seen. Historians still argue about it.

maths.problem: In a photo from How Much of the Moon Is Lit, the ball is 4.8 cm wide. Its bare part is 1.2 cm wide. What percent is lit? Which floor mark was it?
maths.answer: 25 percent. That is the 60 degree mark.
maths.explain: 1.2 divided by 4.8 is 0.25, which is 25 percent. A quarter of the face is lit when the Moon is 60 degrees from the Sun.
maths.context: In How Much of the Moon Is Lit, you measure two widths on each photo: the whole ball and its bare part.
maths.why_maths: A percent lets you compare photos of different sizes, because it does not depend on how big the ball looks.

maths.problem: The percent lit was 7 at 30 degrees and 25 at 60 degrees. Without measuring, what should it be at 150 degrees and at 120 degrees? Say why.
maths.answer: About 93 percent at 150 degrees and 75 percent at 120 degrees.
maths.explain: The part that is lit at 30 degrees is the same size as the part that is dark at 150 degrees. So the two lit shares add up to 100. 100 minus 7 is 93, and 100 minus 25 is 75.
maths.context: In How Much of the Moon Is Lit, the ball stood at seven marks from 0 to 180 degrees. The results have a pattern.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets you predict a result before you measure it, and check a result that looks odd.

maths.problem: The Moon moves about 12 degrees further from the Sun each day. How many days after Amavasya is it 90 degrees from the Sun? Which phase is that?
maths.answer: About 7 and a half days. It is the growing half Moon.
maths.explain: 90 divided by 12 is 7.5. Halfway through Shukla Paksha the Moon is a half Moon.
maths.context: In How Much of the Moon Is Lit, each floor mark stood for a number of days after Amavasya.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the angle by the daily step turns a place on the Moon's path into a date.

maths.problem: A bulb 5 cm wide hangs 200 cm above the paper. Where should the dark shadow of a chana 6 mm wide end?
maths.answer: About 240 mm, or 24 cm, above the paper.
maths.explain: 200 divided by 5 is 40. The dark shadow is 40 widths long. 6 mm times 40 is 240 mm.
maths.context: In The Shadow That Runs Out, the length of a dark shadow in widths matched the lamp's distance divided by the lamp's width.
maths.why_maths: The rule is a ratio, so one division and one multiplication predict the shadow of any small thing under any round lamp.

maths.problem: In the made-up results of The Shadow That Runs Out, the button gave 345 ÷ 12, which is about 29. The lamp's number was 30. Give one reason for the difference.
maths.answer: The last tiny dark dot is hard to see, so people stop lifting a little too early.
maths.explain: A height that is a little too small gives a number that is a little too small. A difference of 1 in 30 is about 3 parts in 100, which is small for a test done by eye.
maths.context: In The Shadow That Runs Out, you judge by eye the moment when the dark middle of a shadow vanishes.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the measured number with the expected one shows how big the error is, and points to where it comes from.

maths.problem: The Moon is 3,474 km wide. In sunlight a dark shadow is about 108 widths long. How long is the Moon's dark shadow? Does it reach ground that is 399,000 km away?
maths.answer: About 375,000 km. No, it ends about 24,000 km short.
maths.explain: 3,474 times 108 is 375,192, which is about 375,000 km. 399,000 minus 375,000 is 24,000. The dark shadow ends above the ground, so people see a ring eclipse.
maths.context: In The Shadow That Runs Out, every dark shadow ended a fixed number of widths behind the thing. In sunlight that number is about 108.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the Moon's width by 108 shows why the Moon's shadow only just reaches the Earth, and sometimes does not.

maths.problem: Eclipse pairs come about 177 days apart. A lunar eclipse was on 3 March 2026. On about which date was the next lunar eclipse?
maths.answer: About 27 August 2026. The real date was 28 August 2026.
maths.explain: From 3 March to 3 September is 184 days. Going back 7 days gives 27 August. The real eclipse came one day later, because six Moon months are a little over 177 days.
maths.context: In Eclipse Detective, the 12 eclipses of 2024 to 2026 came in pairs, and the pairs were about 177 days apart.
maths.why_maths: Counting days on a calendar turns the pattern into a date that can be checked against the real sky.

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home, so treat the expected results as likely, not certain. How Much of the Moon Is Lit (core) needs a ball, a dark sock, a string and about 2.5 metres by 1 metre of floor. The sock must end exactly at the widest part of the ball, and the bare half must face the wall flat on at every mark. The expected percents are 0, 7, 25, 50, 75, 93 and 100, and results within 5 of these are good. A phone photo is the easiest way to measure, and a ruler at arm's length also works. The Shadow That Runs Out (core) needs one bare round bulb and a dark room. A tube light will not work, because it is long and not round. The moment when the dark middle vanishes is a judgement, so each height is measured twice. With a bulb 6 cm wide and 180 cm away, the number should come out between 25 and 32. Its sunlight step is extra, and the unit works without it. A Black Card in the Dark works only when the black card is the only lit thing in view. Light that spills onto a wall weakens the result. Viewers usually call the card pale grey, and not everyone calls it white. The child, who knows the card is black, may see it darker. The Coin Eclipse needs a plate, a coin and 3 metres of room. Fit the Earth's Shadow needs a photograph of a partial lunar eclipse from the web or a book. The edge of the shadow is blurred, so answers from 2 to 3 and a half Moons are all good. Eclipse Detective uses the real eclipse dates of 2024 to 2026 by world time. In India a date can differ by one day. Aristarchus's Angle needs a protractor and 3.5 metres of floor. The crossing at 89 degrees can fall anywhere from 2 to 4 metres, and that spread is the lesson. Swap Places reuses the sock ball. Both games are written out in full, with 24 and 20 cards, and each can be played alone. The Angle Diary needs a view of the western sky on five evenings. A fist is a rough ruler, and an error of 10 degrees is normal. An Eclipse Machine uses the family's own number from The Shadow That Runs Out. A True-Scale Eclipse on a Stick needs direct sunlight, and the peppercorn's shadow on the ball is a faint smudge, which is true to life. Nothing needs a garden or an animal. Nobody looks at the Sun in any step. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026 against NASA, Vassar College, the Indian Institute of Astrophysics and other sources: the Moon's size and distances, the shadow lengths, the 2009 and 2019 eclipse details, the saros dates, Aristarchus and Cassini, the Maria Mitchell and Annie Maunder lines, Talni, Kodaikanal and Proba-3. Softened or removed: the Moon's nearest and furthest distances, the speed of the Moon's dark spot, the streamer length, the age of the Babylon records, the Earth's brightness from the Moon, the verse numbers, the Meeus citation, the Bengaluru planetarium link, the Kongu note, and the 1.4 metre disc (one source). The story is made up. The three Roots teachings are paraphrased. The three videos have no confirmed ids.
